name: Allah, Before All Creation
summary: Before anything else existed, Allah alone existed, with nothing beside Him. The Prophet (SAW) said that Allah's Throne was then upon the water, and that He wrote everything that would happen in the Book before creating the heavens and the earth.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3191
references.gist: Imran ibn Husain narrates the Prophet said: Allah existed and nothing existed before Him, and His Throne was upon the water; He then wrote everything in the Book and created the heavens and the earth.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 7418
references.gist: A parallel narration of the same hadith describing Allah's existence before all else and the Throne upon the water.

name: The Pen and the Preserved Tablet
summary: Hadith literature states the first thing Allah created was the Pen, commanded to write everything decreed until the Hour. Sahih Muslim records that Allah ordained the measures of all creation fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, while His Throne was upon the water. The Quran opens Surah Al-Qalam by swearing an oath by the pen and what is written.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 4700
references.gist: States the first thing Allah created was the Pen, commanded to write everything that would happen until the Hour.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2653b
references.gist: States Allah wrote the measures of all creation fifty thousand years before creating the heavens and the earth, while His Throne was upon the water.

references.label: Surah Al-Qalam 68:1
references.gist: Opens with an oath by the pen and what is written.

name: The Throne and the Footstool
summary: Al-Arsh (the Throne) and al-Kursi (the Footstool) are two distinct creations, not the same thing, a common confusion. The Kursi is described as vast, encompassing the heavens and the earth, while classical commentary holds the Arsh is far greater still; their true nature is known to Allah alone.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:7
references.gist: States Allah's Throne was upon the water when He created the heavens and the earth.

references.label: Ayat al-Kursi, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:255
references.gist: States His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them tires Him not.

name: Creation of the Heavens and the Earth
summary: The Quran repeatedly states that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, while His Throne was upon the water, and that He is not touched by fatigue.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:54
references.gist: States Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself above the Throne.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:7
references.gist: States Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, while His Throne was upon the water.

references.label: Surah Fussilat 41:9-12
references.gist: Describes the creation of the earth in two days and the heavens in two more, detailing the six-day process.

references.label: Surah Qaf 50:38
references.gist: States that Allah created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Him.

name: The Angels
summary: Angels were created from light, as opposed to jinn, created from fire, and Adam, created from clay, according to a hadith in Sahih Muslim. The Quran describes angels as never disobeying Allah in what He commands them, carrying out His orders exactly.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2996
references.gist: Aisha narrates the Prophet said angels were created from light, jinn from a smokeless flame of fire, and Adam from what has been described to you (clay).

references.label: Surah At-Tahrim 66:6
references.gist: Describes angels as stern and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do as they are commanded.

name: Jibril (Gabriel)
summary: The angel entrusted with bringing revelation down to the prophets, including the Quran to Muhammad (SAW). The Quran names him directly and states he brought the revelation down by Allah's leave.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:97
references.gist: Names Jibril (Gabriel) directly, stating he brought the Quran down upon the Prophet's heart by Allah's permission.

name: Mikail (Michael)
summary: Named directly in the Quran alongside Jibril as one of Allah's angels. Classical commentary associates him with provision and rain, though the Quran itself names him without detailing his specific duty.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:98
references.gist: Names Mikail (Michael) alongside Jibril as an enemy of Allah's enemies, without detailing his specific role.

name: Israfil
summary: The angel who will blow the trumpet to signal the Hour and the Resurrection. The Quran describes the blowing of the trumpet in several places but does not itself name the angel; a hadith does name him directly, describing the Prophet's companions asking how he could be at ease knowing that 'the Angel of the Trumpet (Israfil) has put his lips to the Trumpet and is waiting for the order to blow it.' So the name Israfil is hadith-attested, not found in the Quranic text.

references.label: Riyad as-Salihin 409
references.gist: States the Angel of the Trumpet has put his lips to the Trumpet and is waiting for the order to blow it; this is the primary hadith basis for the name Israfil, which the Quran itself does not use.

name: Kiraman Katibin, the Recording Angels
summary: The Quran describes two angels appointed over every person, one on each side, recording everything they say and do; nothing goes unrecorded.

references.label: Surah Al-Infitar 82:10-12
references.gist: States that noble recording angels are appointed over every person and know whatever they do.

references.label: Surah Qaf 50:17-18
references.gist: States that two scribes sit on the right and the left, and a person utters no word without a watcher ready to record it.

name: The Angel of Death
summary: The Quran states that the angel of death, entrusted with each person, will take their soul, after which they return to their Lord. The Quran refers to him only by title, malak al-mawt, the angel of death, without giving him a personal name.

references.label: Surah As-Sajdah 32:11
references.gist: States the angel of death, put in charge of you, will take your souls, then you will be returned to your Lord.

name: Munkar and Nakir
summary: Two angels named in hadith, not in the Quran, who question the deceased in the grave about their Lord, their religion, and their prophet. See the Trial and Punishment of the Grave under End Times for the fuller account of the questioning itself.

references.label: Jami at-Tirmidhi 1071
references.gist: Names the two angels Munkar and Nakir directly, who come to the deceased in the grave and question them about the man (the Prophet) sent to them.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 4753
references.gist: Describes the three questions asked in the grave: who is your Lord, what is your religion, who is this man sent to you.

name: Malik, Keeper of Hell
summary: The Quran names Malik directly as the angel in charge of Hell, whom its inhabitants will call out to.

references.label: Surah Az-Zukhruf 43:77
references.gist: Describes the people of the Fire calling out, 'O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us,' naming Malik directly as Hell's keeper.

name: The Bearers of the Throne (Hamalat al-Arsh)
summary: Angels who carry Allah's Throne and others who surround it, glorifying their Lord, believing in Him, and asking forgiveness for those who believe, described on the Day of Resurrection as eight in number bearing it above the rest.

references.label: Surah Ghafir 40:7
references.gist: The angels who carry the Throne, and those around it, glorify their Lord, believe in Him, and seek forgiveness for the believers.

references.label: Surah Al-Haqqah 69:17
references.gist: States that on that Day, eight angels will bear the Throne of your Lord above them.

name: The Keepers of Paradise
summary: Angels stationed at Paradise's gates open them for its people and greet them, saying peace be upon you, you have done well, so enter it to remain forever. Angels also enter upon its people from every gate, greeting them with peace for their patient endurance. No individual keeper is named in the Quran or in any authentic hadith.

references.label: Surah Az-Zumar 39:73
references.gist: The keepers of Paradise greet its people as its gates are opened for them, saying peace be upon you, you have done well, so enter it to remain forever.

references.label: Surah Ar-Ra'd 13:23-24
references.gist: Angels enter upon the people of Paradise from every gate, greeting them with peace for what they patiently endured.

name: The Jinn
summary: The Quran states the jinn were created before mankind, from a smokeless flame of fire, distinct from angels, made of light, and humans, made of clay.

references.label: Surah Al-Hijr 15:27
references.gist: States the jinn were created before Adam from the smokeless fire of a scorching wind.

references.label: Surah Ar-Rahman 55:15
references.gist: States the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire.

name: Iblis
summary: The Quran states plainly that Iblis was of the jinn, correcting the common misconception that he was a fallen angel. When Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, they all did except Iblis, who refused out of arrogance and disobeyed his Lord.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:50
references.gist: States Iblis was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord, correcting the common assumption that he was a fallen angel.

name: Adam (AS)
summary: The first human being and prophet. Allah created him with His own hand, taught him the names of all things, and commanded the angels to prostrate to him. He and his wife dwelt in Paradise until Iblis deceived them into eating from the forbidden tree; Allah accepted their repentance and sent them to the earth.

family.name: Hawwa (Eve)
family.note: Not named in the Quran text, which refers to her only as 'his wife.' The name is, however, used directly in an authentic hadith in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet says: 'Were it not for Hawwa, no woman would ever have been unfaithful to her husband.'

family.name: Not named in the Quran or in any authentic hadith
family.note: Quran 5:27-31 tells the story of Adam's two sons and the first murder without naming either of them. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari also references 'the first son of Adam' who began the practice of murder, likewise without naming him.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:30-39
references.gist: Covers Adam's creation, the angels being taught to prostrate before him, Iblis's refusal, and the fall to earth after the forbidden tree.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:19-25
references.gist: Covers Satan's deception over the forbidden tree, Adam and his wife's nakedness being exposed, and their being sent down to earth.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3326
references.gist: Describes Adam's creation and height (sixty cubits), and that people have since continued to diminish in stature.

tale.intro: The story of the first human being begins not on earth but in the divine council, where Allah announced a plan the angels did not yet understand.

chapters.heading: Creation and the Teaching of the Names
chapters.narrative: Allah told the angels that He was going to place a vicegerent on the earth. The angels asked whether He would place there one who would spread corruption and shed blood, while they glorified and sanctified Him. Allah replied that He knew what they did not know. He had already told them He would create a human being from clay taken from altered, dried mud, and that once He had proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit, they were to fall down before him. When Adam was formed, Allah taught him the names of all things, then presented these things to the angels and asked them to name them if they were truthful. The angels admitted they had no knowledge except what He had taught them. Allah then told Adam to inform the angels of the names, and when he did, Allah pointed out that He knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and knows what they reveal and what they conceal.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:30-33
references.gist: Allah announces He will place a vicegerent on earth, the angels question it, and Adam is shown to know the names of things that even the angels do not know.

references.label: Surah Al-Hijr 15:26-29
references.gist: Allah describes creating a human being from clay of altered black mud, to be proportioned and given a breath of His spirit.

chapters.heading: The Prostration of the Angels and Iblis's Refusal
chapters.narrative: Allah commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam, and all of them did so except Iblis, who refused out of arrogance and became one of the disbelievers. When Allah asked what had prevented him from prostrating, Iblis said he was better than Adam, since he had been created from fire while Adam was created from clay. Allah told him to get down from that station, for it was not his place to be arrogant there, and he was cast out and cursed. Iblis then asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection, and it was granted him. He vowed that because Allah had put him in error, he would lie in wait for Adam's descendants on the straight path, coming at them from before and behind and from their right and their left, so that Allah would find most of them ungrateful. Allah replied that Iblis would be driven out in disgrace, and that He would fill Hell with him and all who followed him.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:11-18
references.gist: The angels are commanded to prostrate to Adam; Iblis refuses, claims superiority through fire over clay, is expelled, asks for and receives respite, and vows to attack mankind from every direction.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:71-78
references.gist: A parallel account of Iblis's refusal to prostrate, his claim of being better than Adam, and Allah's curse upon him until the Day of Judgment.

chapters.heading: Paradise, the Forbidden Tree, and Satan's Deception
chapters.narrative: Allah settled Adam and his wife in Paradise and told them to eat freely from wherever they wished, but not to approach one particular tree, or they would be among the wrongdoers. Satan whispered to them, wanting to expose to them what had been hidden of their nakedness, telling them their Lord had only forbidden the tree to keep them from becoming angels or immortals, and swearing to them that he was sincerely advising them. He called it the tree of eternity, a kingdom that never decays. Deceived by this guile, they ate from the tree, and their nakedness became apparent to them, so they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:35
references.gist: Adam and his wife are told to dwell in the Garden and eat freely except from one tree.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:19-22
references.gist: Satan whispers to Adam and his wife, swears he is sincere, and deceives them into eating from the tree, after which their nakedness is exposed to them.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:120-121
references.gist: Satan tempts Adam specifically with the promise of a tree of eternity, and Adam eats and disobeys, and his nakedness becomes apparent.

chapters.heading: The Fall to Earth and the Acceptance of Repentance
chapters.narrative: Adam and his wife said their Lord, they had wronged themselves, and if He did not forgive them and have mercy upon them, they would surely be among the losers. Allah told them to descend from the Garden, some as enemies to others, with a dwelling place and provision on earth for a time; there they would live, there they would die, and from it they would be brought forth again. Then Adam received words from his Lord, and Allah turned to him in forgiveness, for He is the Accepting of Repentance, the Merciful. Allah told him that guidance would come to his descendants, and whoever followed that guidance would not go astray nor suffer, while whoever turned away from it would have a narrow, straitened life.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:23-25
references.gist: Adam and his wife confess their wrongdoing and ask forgiveness, and are told they will have a dwelling place on earth for a time.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:36-37
references.gist: Adam and his wife are sent down to earth; Adam receives words from his Lord and his repentance is accepted.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:122-124
references.gist: Allah chooses Adam, forgives him, gives him guidance, and promises that whoever follows that guidance will not go astray or suffer.

chapters.heading: The Two Sons of Adam
chapters.narrative: Adam's two sons each offered a sacrifice; it was accepted from one and not the other. The one whose offering was rejected said he would surely kill his brother. His brother answered that Allah only accepts from those who are mindful of Him, and that even if he were attacked he would not raise his hand in return, for he feared Allah, the Lord of all worlds; he would rather his brother bear the sin of killing him, along with his own sins, than that he himself sin by killing. His brother's soul persuaded him to kill him, and he did, becoming one of the losers. Not knowing what to do with the corpse, he watched a crow scratch the ground to show him how to bury his brother's body, and he cried out in regret that he could not even do as the crow had done. Because of this, it was decreed that whoever kills a soul unjustly, it is as if he had killed all mankind, and whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all mankind. The Quran does not name these two sons anywhere in this account.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:27-32
references.gist: The two unnamed sons of Adam offer sacrifices, one is accepted and not the other, the rejected one kills his brother and learns from a crow how to bury him, and the principle is laid down that killing one innocent soul is like killing all mankind.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3335
references.gist: The Prophet Muhammad said that a share of the burden of every unjust killing falls upon the first son of Adam, since he was the first to establish the practice of murder.

name: The Primordial Covenant
summary: The Quran describes Allah bringing forth every one of Adam's descendants from his loins before this world began and making each of them testify to His Lordship, so that no one could claim ignorance of Him on the Day of Judgment. Hadith describe every child as still born upon this natural disposition (fitrah) toward belief, though upbringing can turn them away from it.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:172-173
references.gist: Describes Allah bringing forth the descendants from the loins of the Children of Adam and making them testify, 'Yes, You are our Lord,' a covenant taken so no one could plead ignorance on the Day of Resurrection.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1359
references.gist: The Prophet says every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition toward belief), and it is his parents who make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian.

name: Idris (AS)
lineage: Traditionally placed among the descendants of Adam (AS), prior to Nuh (AS); the Quran itself does not specify his lineage.
summary: A man of truth and a prophet whom Allah raised to a high station. Traditional accounts, not the Quran itself, place him several generations before Nuh (AS) in Adam's line.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:56-57
references.gist: Describes Idris as a man of truth and a prophet, raised by Allah to a high station.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:85-86
references.gist: Names Idris alongside Ismail and Dhul-Kifl as among the patient, admitted into Allah's mercy as righteous.

tale.intro: Of all the prophets named in the Quran, Idris receives the fewest words, but what little is said of him is unambiguous.

chapters.heading: A Truthful Prophet, Raised to a High Station
chapters.narrative: The Quran mentions Idris in only two short passages. It calls him a man of truth and a prophet, and says that Allah raised him to a high station. Elsewhere, he is named alongside Ismail and Dhul-Kifl as one of those who were patient, and who were admitted into Allah's mercy for being among the righteous. The Quran gives no account of specific events in his life, no people he was sent to, and no confrontation he faced, only this description of his character and the honor Allah showed him. Separately, in an authenticated hadith describing the Prophet Muhammad's night journey through the heavens, he is described as meeting a prophet identified as Idris in one of the heavens, who greeted him as a righteous brother and prophet; the hadith explicitly connects this meeting to the Quran's description of Idris as one who was raised to a high station. Beyond this, nothing further about him can be established from the Quran or authenticated hadith, and later traditions add other biographical details about him not repeated here, since they rest on tafsir and Israiliyyat material rather than the Quran or hadith itself.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:56-57
references.gist: Idris is described as a man of truth and a prophet, and Allah says He raised him to a high station.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:85-86
references.gist: Idris is named with Ismail and Dhul-Kifl as among the patient, admitted into Allah's mercy as righteous.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 164a
references.gist: In the narration of the night journey (Isra and Mi'raj), the Prophet Muhammad meets Idris in one of the heavens, who welcomes him, echoing the Quran's description of Idris as one raised to an exalted position.

name: Nuh (AS)
lineage: A descendant of Adam (AS), many generations later.
summary: Sent to call his people to worship Allah alone. The Quran records that he remained among them a thousand years less fifty, inviting them patiently before Allah commanded him to build an ark. Those who disbelieved were destroyed in the flood, while Nuh, his family, and the believers were saved.

provenDates.label: 950 years spent calling his people, before the flood

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:14
references.gist: States Nuh remained among his people a thousand years less fifty.

family.name: Not named in the Quran or in any authentic hadith
family.note: Quran 66:10 refers to her only as 'the wife of Nuh,' described as unfaithful to his message (that verse is this entry's reference); a dedicated search across the major hadith collections found no authentic hadith naming her.

family.name: Not named in the Quran or in any authentic hadith
family.note: Quran 11:42-46 describes an unnamed son who refused to board the ark and was drowned; Allah tells Nuh this son 'is not of your family' in conduct (that passage is this entry's reference); a dedicated search across the major hadith collections found no authentic hadith naming him.

references.label: Surah Nuh 71:1-28
references.gist: Nuh's call to his people, their rejection, and his prayer for their destruction and for his household and the believers.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:25-49
references.gist: Covers Nuh's mission, the building of the ark, the flood, his son's refusal to board, and the ark settling on Mount Judi.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:14
references.gist: States Nuh remained among his people a thousand years less fifty before the Flood overtook them.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4712
references.gist: In the hadith of intercession, Nuh is the first prophet approached and the first to decline, pointing people on to Ibrahim.

tale.intro: Nuh's story is the longest sustained prophetic struggle in the Quran, spanning nearly a millennium of patient warning against near-total rejection.

chapters.heading: Sent to Warn a People Who Would Not Listen
chapters.narrative: Nuh was sent to his people with the command to warn them before a painful punishment came upon them, and he called them to worship Allah alone, since He was their only god. He remained among them, calling them night and day, in public and in private, for what the Quran records as a thousand years less fifty, nearly nine hundred and fifty years. Yet each time he called them toward forgiveness, they only fled further from him, plugging their ears and covering themselves with their garments, persisting in arrogance and pride. When Nuh insisted he was a genuine messenger from the Lord of all the worlds bringing them sincere advice, the leaders among his people answered that he was clearly misguided.

references.label: Surah Nuh 71:1-9
references.gist: Nuh is sent to warn his people and describes calling them night and day, openly and secretly, only for them to flee further and cover their ears.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:14
references.gist: Nuh remained among his people a thousand years less fifty before the Flood overtook them.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:59-61
references.gist: Nuh warns his people to worship Allah alone; the chiefs accuse him of being clearly misguided, and he replies he is a true messenger.

chapters.heading: Mockery and the Command to Build the Ark
chapters.narrative: The people of Nuh insisted they would not believe in him while only the lowest of society followed him, and mocked him further when he began building the ark on dry land, far from any sea. Every time a group of the leading men passed by him at his work, they laughed at him, and he answered that if they were laughing at him now, he would laugh at them in turn later, when they would learn who would be seized by a humiliating punishment. Eventually Nuh cried out to his Lord that he had been overpowered by his people and asked for help, and it was revealed to him that none of his people would believe except those who already had, so he should not grieve over what they had been doing, and should build the ark under Allah's watchful eyes and guidance.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:36-39
references.gist: Allah tells Nuh no more of his people will believe, commands him to build the ark, and the chiefs mock him as he builds it on dry land.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:111-115
references.gist: The people object that only the lowest among them follow Nuh; he answers that he has no knowledge of their social standing, only Allah does.

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:9-10
references.gist: Nuh's people denied him, called him mad, and threatened him, until he cried out to his Lord that he was overpowered and needed help.

chapters.heading: The Flood
chapters.narrative: When Allah's command came, water gushed forth and the heavens opened with pouring rain, while the earth burst with springs, so that the waters met for a matter already decreed. Nuh was commanded to load onto the ark a pair of every kind of creature, along with his family, except those already doomed to drown, and the believers, though only a few had believed with him. The ark sailed under Allah's watchful care, amid waves like mountains, carrying those who had heeded the warning while the rest of the people, including many of Nuh's own kin, were drowned.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:40
references.gist: When the command comes and water gushes forth, Nuh is told to load two of every kind and his family, except the doomed, and only a few had believed with him.

references.label: Surah Al-Mu'minun 23:27
references.gist: Allah instructs Nuh to build the ark and, when the flood comes, to take aboard a pair of every kind and his believing followers.

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:11-14
references.gist: The heavens pour forth water and the earth bursts with springs; the waters meet by a decreed measure, and Nuh is carried on the ark under Allah's watchful care.

chapters.heading: The Son Who Refused to Board
chapters.narrative: As the ark sailed amid towering waves, Nuh called out to his son, who stood apart from the rest, urging him to come aboard and not remain with the disbelievers. His son answered that he would take refuge on a mountain to protect himself from the water. Nuh told him there was no protector that day from Allah's command, except for those on whom He had mercy, and a wave came between them, and his son was among those who drowned. Afterward Nuh pleaded with his Lord, saying his son was of his family and Allah's promise was true. Allah answered that his son was not of the family in the sense Nuh meant, for his conduct was other than righteous, and told Nuh not to ask about matters of which he had no knowledge. Nuh then sought refuge in Allah from asking for what he did not know, and asked for forgiveness and mercy.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:42-47
references.gist: Nuh calls to his son to board the ark; the son refuses, trusting a mountain instead, and drowns; Nuh's plea for him is answered that his conduct disqualified him.

chapters.heading: Mount Judi and Nuh's Prayer
chapters.narrative: When the flood receded, it was said, 'O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold your rain,' and the water subsided, the matter was concluded, and the ark came to rest on Mount Judi. It was then said, 'Away with the wrongdoing people.' Nuh was told to disembark in security and with blessings upon him and upon the communities that would descend from those with him, while other communities would be given worldly enjoyment before a painful punishment eventually touched them. Nuh then prayed to his Lord for forgiveness for himself, for his parents, for whoever entered his house as a believer, and for all believing men and women.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:44
references.gist: The flood recedes, the matter is concluded, and the ark comes to rest on Mount Judi.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:48
references.gist: Nuh is told to disembark in security and blessing, with future generations to be granted temporary worldly enjoyment before facing consequences for wrongdoing.

references.label: Surah Nuh 71:28
references.gist: Nuh prays for forgiveness for himself, his parents, and believing men and women.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3340
references.gist: In the hadith describing intercession on the Day of Resurrection, Nuh is addressed as the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth.

name: Hud (AS)
lineage: Not a descendant of Nuh (AS) by any stated line, but the Quran does place his people, Aad, chronologically after Nuh's: 'and remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh' (7:69), the same wording used for Thamud after Aad. That is a real textual basis for placing him after Nuh here, not a lineage claim.
summary: Sent to the people of Aad, calling them to worship Allah alone and abandon their idols. When they persisted in disbelief and arrogance, Allah destroyed them with a violent, roaring wind, while Hud and the believers were saved.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:50-60
references.gist: Covers Hud's call to the people of 'Aad, their rejection, and their destruction.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:65-72
references.gist: Covers Hud's warning to 'Aad and Allah saving him and the believers from the punishment that followed.

tale.intro: After the flood, a new and powerful nation arose in Nuh's place, and to them Allah sent one of their own.

chapters.heading: Sent to the People of 'Aad
chapters.narrative: Allah sent Hud to the people of 'Aad as their brother. He called them to worship Allah alone, since they had no other god, and warned them, but the disbelieving chiefs among his people accused him of foolishness and thought him a liar. Hud replied there was no foolishness in him; he was a messenger from the Lord of all the worlds, bringing them his Lord's messages as a trustworthy adviser. He told them he asked no reward from them, for his reward was with the One who had created him, and urged them to ask forgiveness of their Lord and turn back to Him, promising that He would send abundant rain and increase them in strength. He also warned them at the sand dunes where they lived, reminding them that warners had come both before and after him with the same message: worship none but Allah, for he feared for them the punishment of a great Day.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:65-68
references.gist: Hud is sent to 'Aad, calls them to worship Allah alone, and is accused of foolishness by the disbelieving chiefs.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:50-52
references.gist: Hud calls his people to worship Allah, seek His forgiveness, and repent, promising increased rain and strength if they do.

references.label: Surah Al-Ahqaf 46:21
references.gist: Hud warns his people at the sand dunes, noting warners had come both before and after him with the same message.

chapters.heading: Monuments, Fortresses, and Arrogant Rejection
chapters.narrative: Hud rebuked his people for building landmarks on every high place out of vanity, and for constructing fortresses as though they would live forever, and for seizing people violently, like tyrants, when they attacked. He urged them to fear the One who had given them cattle, children, gardens, and springs, warning that he feared for them the punishment of a terrible Day. His people answered that he had not brought them clear evidence, and that they would not abandon their gods merely on his word, suggesting instead that one of their gods had struck him with madness. Hud called Allah to witness, and them as well, that he was free of anything they associated with Him. When they demanded he bring the punishment he threatened if he were truthful, he told them that knowledge of its timing belonged to Allah alone, and that he saw they were behaving in ignorance.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:128-135
references.gist: Hud rebukes 'Aad for building vain monuments, fortresses, and acting as tyrants, urging them to fear the One who gave them their blessings.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:53-54
references.gist: His people reject his message for lack of evidence and accuse him of having been struck mad by their gods; Hud disclaims any part in their idols.

references.label: Surah Al-Ahqaf 46:22-23
references.gist: The people demand the promised punishment; Hud says only Allah knows its timing and that they are acting in ignorance.

chapters.heading: The Violent Wind
chapters.narrative: When the people finally saw a cloud approaching their valleys, they rejoiced, believing it would bring them rain. Instead, it was the very punishment they had impatiently demanded: a wind carrying painful torment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord, so that by morning nothing could be seen except the ruins of their own dwellings. The Quran describes this as a screaming, violent wind that struck them on a day of continuous misfortune, tearing people from the ground as though they were uprooted trunks of palm trees, and states that it raged against them for seven nights and eight days without pause, leaving them lying overthrown, until no remains of them could be seen.

references.label: Surah Al-Ahqaf 46:24-25
references.gist: The people mistake the approaching punishment for a rain cloud; the wind destroys everything, leaving only their ruined dwellings visible.

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:18-21
references.gist: 'Aad is struck by a screaming wind on a day of continuous misfortune, uprooting people like fallen palm trunks.

references.label: Surah Al-Haqqah 69:6-8
references.gist: The violent wind rages against 'Aad for seven nights and eight days, leaving them overthrown with no remains visible afterward.

chapters.heading: Deliverance of Hud and the Believers
chapters.narrative: When Allah's command came to pass, He saved Hud and those who had believed with him through His mercy, sparing them from the harsh punishment that befell the rest, and cutting off the last remnant of those who had denied His signs and refused to believe. The story closes as a sign, though most people still would not believe, while Allah remains the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:72
references.gist: Allah saves Hud and those with him by His mercy, and destroys those who denied His signs.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:58
references.gist: When the command comes, Hud and the believers with him are saved by mercy from Allah, spared the harsh punishment.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:139-140
references.gist: The people are destroyed for their denial; the account closes noting this as a sign, though most do not believe.

placementNote.text: Hud sits one row after Nuh because the Quran identifies 'Aad, the people he was sent to, as successors who settled the land after the people of Nuh.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:69
references.gist: Reminds 'Aad that Allah made them successors after the people of Nuh.

name: Salih (AS)
lineage: Not a descendant of Hud (AS) by any stated line, but the Quran places his people, Thamud, chronologically after Aad, using the same 'successors after' construction as Hud's placement after Nuh: 'and made you successors after Aad' (7:74). A real textual basis for placing him after Hud here, not a lineage claim.
summary: Sent to the people of Thamud after Hud. Allah brought forth a she-camel from solid rock as a sign for them, with instructions to let her graze unharmed; when they killed her in defiance, a violent blast destroyed the whole people three days later, sparing only Salih and the believers.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:61-68
references.gist: Covers Salih's call to Thamud, the she-camel as a sign, and the blast that destroyed the people after they hamstrung her.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:141-159
references.gist: Covers Salih's warning to Thamud and the she-camel given to them as a trial.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:73-79
references.gist: Covers Salih's mission to Thamud and the earthquake that struck them after they killed the she-camel.

tale.intro: In the rock-cut homeland of Thamud, another prophet came from among his own people, bringing with him a sign unlike any other.

chapters.heading: Sent to the People of Thamud
chapters.narrative: Allah sent Salih to the people of Thamud as their brother. He called them to worship Allah alone, reminded them that Allah had produced them from the earth and settled them in it, and urged them to seek His forgiveness and turn back to Him, for his Lord was near and responsive. He told them he asked no payment from them for delivering the message, for his reward came only from the Lord of all the worlds, and insisted he was a trustworthy messenger to them.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:73
references.gist: Salih is sent to Thamud, calling them to worship Allah alone and announcing that clear evidence has come to them.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:61
references.gist: Salih reminds his people that Allah made them from the earth and settled them there, and calls them to seek His forgiveness.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:141-145
references.gist: Salih identifies himself as a trustworthy messenger who asks no payment for his message.

chapters.heading: The She-Camel as a Sign
chapters.narrative: Salih reminded his people of the comfort they already enjoyed, gardens, springs, crops, and date palms with soft, laden clusters, and homes they skillfully carved out of the mountains, and warned them not to follow those who caused corruption in the land. As a clear sign from their Lord, a she-camel was given to them; Salih told them to leave her to graze freely in Allah's land and not to touch her with harm, or a painful punishment would seize them. Allah declared that the she-camel was sent specifically as a trial for them, and that the available water was to be shared between her and them, with each having an appointed turn to drink.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:146-152
references.gist: Salih reminds Thamud of their comfortable life and skillfully carved mountain homes, warning them against corruption.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:73
references.gist: The she-camel is given as a sign, with instructions to leave her to graze and not harm her.

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:27-28
references.gist: The she-camel is sent as a trial, with the water shared between her and the people on an appointed schedule.

chapters.heading: The Hamstringing of the Camel
chapters.narrative: Despite the warning, the people hamstrung the she-camel, defying the order of their Lord, and challenged Salih to bring the punishment he had promised if he was truly a messenger. Rallying together, they called upon one of their own, who took up a blade and cut the camel's legs. Having done this, they became regretful, but it was too late.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:77
references.gist: The people hamstring the she-camel and defiantly challenge Salih to bring the promised punishment.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:157
references.gist: Having hamstrung the she-camel, the people became regretful.

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:29
references.gist: The people call upon one of their own, who takes up a blade and hamstrings the camel.

chapters.heading: The Blast and the Deliverance of the Believers
chapters.narrative: After the camel was killed, Salih told his people to enjoy themselves in their homes for three more days, a promise that would not fail. When Allah's command came, He saved Salih and those who had believed with him through His mercy, sparing them from the disgrace of that day, for his Lord is the Powerful, the Exalted in Might. A mighty blast then seized the wrongdoers, and by morning they lay motionless, fallen face-down within their own homes, as though they had never lived there and flourished. Salih turned away from them, saying he had delivered his Lord's message and given them sincere advice, but they had not loved those who advised them.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:65-67
references.gist: Salih gives Thamud three days' respite; when the command comes, Salih and the believers are saved and the wrongdoers are struck down by a blast.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:78-79
references.gist: An earthquake seizes the people, leaving them fallen in their homes; Salih laments that they rejected his sincere advice.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shams 91:14-15
references.gist: Because of their sin, their Lord brought destruction down upon them equally, without fear of consequence.

placementNote.text: Salih sits one row after Hud because the Quran identifies Thamud, the people he was sent to, as successors after 'Aad.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:74
references.gist: Reminds Thamud that Allah made them successors after 'Aad and settled them in the land.

name: Lut (AS)
lineage: The nephew of Ibrahim (AS), son of Ibrahim's brother Haran, not his descendant; he is not a link in the generational chain shown in this tree.
summary: The nephew of Ibrahim (AS), who migrated with him and was later sent as a messenger to the people of Sodom. He warned them against their sexual immorality; when they refused to relent, Allah's angels evacuated Lut and his believing family by night before overturning the cities, leaving Lut's own wife among the destroyed for her disbelief.

placementNote.text: Lut shares this row with Ibrahim, rather than sitting on a line of his own, because the Quran narrates them as contemporaries: he believed in Ibrahim, and the same messenger-angels who brought Ibrahim news of a son went straight on to Lut's people.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:26
references.gist: States that Lut believed in Ibrahim.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:69-77
references.gist: The same messenger-angels visit Ibrahim with good news, then go on to Lut.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:69-83
references.gist: Covers the angels' visit to Ibrahim, then to Lut, and the destruction of Lut's people.

references.label: Surah Al-Hijr 15:57-77
references.gist: Covers the angels' visit to Lut, his people's approach to his house, and the towns being overturned.

tale.intro: Even as angels journeyed to bring Ibrahim news of a son, they carried with them a second, graver purpose concerning the towns where his nephew Lut lived.

chapters.heading: Ibrahim's Plea for the Doomed Towns
chapters.narrative: When Allah's messengers came to Ibrahim with good news, they also told him they had been sent to the people of Lut. Once his fear had subsided and the good news had reached him, Ibrahim began to plead with them on behalf of Lut's people, for he was forbearing, tender-hearted, and ever turning back to Allah. The angels told him to abandon this plea, for the command of his Lord had already come, and a punishment that could not be turned back was about to fall upon them, since those people had become wrongdoers.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:74-76
references.gist: After hearing good news, Ibrahim pleads with the angels on behalf of Lut's people, but is told the irreversible punishment has already been decreed.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:31
references.gist: The messengers tell Ibrahim they are going to destroy the people of that town for their wrongdoing.

chapters.heading: Sent to a People Given to a New Wickedness
chapters.narrative: Lut said to his people that they were committing an indecency no people before them in all the worlds had ever committed: they approached men with desire instead of women, abandoning the wives Allah had created for them. Beyond this, the Quran describes them as people who also cut off travelers on the road and committed evil openly in their gatherings. When Lut confronted them with this, his people's only response was to demand that he bring down Allah's punishment on them if he was telling the truth.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:80-81
references.gist: Lut confronts his people over an unprecedented indecency: approaching men with desire instead of women.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:165-166
references.gist: Lut asks why they approach men and abandon the wives Allah created for them.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:29
references.gist: Lut's people are also accused of waylaying travelers and committing evil openly in their gatherings, and respond by demanding the punishment.

chapters.heading: The Angels Visit Lut in Human Form
chapters.narrative: When Allah's messengers came to Lut in human form, he was distressed on their account and felt unable to protect them, saying it was a difficult day. His people came rushing toward his house, since they had long been in the habit of committing such deeds, and Lut pleaded with them to fear Allah and not disgrace him in front of his guests, asking if there was not one reasonable man among them. The angels then revealed themselves as messengers of his Lord, telling him his people would not be able to touch him, and instructed him to leave with his family during the night, without anyone looking back, except his wife, who would meet the same fate as the rest.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:77-79
references.gist: The angels arrive in human form; Lut is distressed as his people rush toward his house, and he pleads with them not to disgrace him before his guests.

references.label: Surah Al-Hijr 15:67-71
references.gist: The people of the city come to Lut's house in excitement, and he pleads with them not to shame him before his guests.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:33
references.gist: The messengers tell Lut not to fear or grieve, for they will save him and his family, except his wife.

chapters.heading: The Departure and the Fate of Lut's Wife
chapters.narrative: The angels told Lut that they were indeed messengers of his Lord, and that his people would never be able to reach him, so he should depart with his family during the night and let none of them turn to look back, except his wife, who would be struck by what struck the rest of the people, at daybreak. Lut left with his family and was saved, along with them, except his wife, who remained behind among those who were destroyed.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:81
references.gist: The angels instruct Lut to depart by night without looking back, warning that his wife will share the fate of the destroyed people.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:170-171
references.gist: Lut and his family are saved, except an old woman among those who remained behind, his wife.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:83
references.gist: Lut and his family are saved except his wife, who is among those who remained behind.

chapters.heading: The Destruction of the Towns
chapters.narrative: When Allah's command came, the towns were turned upside down, their highest part made their lowest, and they were struck with a rain of stones of layered, baked clay, marked from their Lord, a punishment never far from wrongdoers. A single blast seized them at sunrise, and only Lut's family was saved before the destruction came at dawn. The Quran notes that the ruins of these towns lay along a road still known and traveled, a lasting sign for those who understand.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:82-83
references.gist: The towns are overturned and struck with stones of layered clay marked from Allah, a punishment never far from wrongdoers.

references.label: Surah Al-Hijr 15:73-77
references.gist: A blast seizes the towns at sunrise, and their location on a known road is noted as a lasting sign.

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:34
references.gist: A storm of stones is sent upon them, except the family of Lut, who are saved before dawn.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:58
references.gist: A rain of stones falls upon them, an evil rain for a people who had been warned.

name: Ibrahim (AS)
lineage: A descendant of Nuh (AS), many generations later.
summary: Known as Khalil Allah, the close friend of Allah. He broke his people's idols to show they could not defend themselves, and was thrown into a fire that Allah commanded to be cool and safe for him. He later built the Kaaba together with his son Isma'il.

family.name: Sarah
family.note: Not explicitly named in the Quran text itself; referred to only as 'his wife' in the passages about Ishaq's birth (11:71, 51:29). The name Sarah is well established in hadith and tafsir tradition, including Sahih al-Bukhari 3358.

family.name: Hajar
family.note: Named directly in Sahih al-Bukhari, both in the account of how she came to Ibrahim's household (3358) and in the account of Zamzam and building the Kaaba with Isma'il (3364). Not named in the Quran text itself.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:125
references.gist: States that Allah took Ibrahim as a khalil (close friend).

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:51-70
references.gist: Covers Ibrahim breaking the idols, being thrown into the fire, and Allah making the fire cool and safe for him.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:124-127
references.gist: Covers Ibrahim being tested and made a leader for mankind, and raising the foundations of the House with Isma'il.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3364
references.gist: Ibn Abbas's long narration of Ibrahim leaving Hajar and infant Isma'il near the future site of the Ka'ba, and the opening of the Zamzam spring.

tale.intro: Ibrahim (AS) is the prophet whose story the Quran returns to more than almost any other: his confrontation with idolatry, his trials, and his founding role at Makkah run through many surahs.

chapters.heading: A Nation of Idols
chapters.narrative: Ibrahim grew up among a people, including his father Azar, who carved idols and worshipped them. He confronted his father directly, asking why he worshipped something that could neither hear, see, nor help him at all, and warned him gently that he feared punishment would touch him if he continued. His father threatened to stone him and told him to leave. Ibrahim also challenged his wider community, asking them plainly what they were worshipping and telling them their idols and their forefathers' idols were in clear error.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:41-48
references.gist: Ibrahim's dialogue with his father, questioning idol worship; his father threatens to stone him and tells him to leave.

references.label: Surah Al-An'am 6:74
references.gist: Ibrahim tells his father Azar he has taken idols as gods, and sees him and his people in clear error.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:52-56
references.gist: Ibrahim asks his father and people what these statues are that they are devoted to, and calls their worship clear error.

chapters.heading: This Is My Lord
chapters.narrative: In a formative moment described in the Quran, Ibrahim looked at the night sky as if reasoning aloud with his people. Seeing a star, he said, this is my Lord, but when it set he said he did not love things that disappear. Seeing the moon rise, he said the same, but when it set he said that without his Lord's guidance he would be among the astray. Seeing the sun rise, he said this is my Lord, this is greater, but when it too set, he declared himself free of everything they associated with Allah and turned his face to the One who created the heavens and the earth.

references.label: Surah Al-An'am 6:75-79
references.gist: Ibrahim's progression from star, to moon, to sun, rejecting each as it sets, then declaring pure devotion to the Creator.

chapters.heading: Smashing the Idols
chapters.narrative: While his people were away, Ibrahim went to their idols and broke all of them except the largest one, so that they might turn to it and question it. When they returned and found the destruction, they asked who had done this to their gods, and were told a young man called Ibrahim had spoken against them. Brought before the people, Ibrahim pointed to the largest idol and said, sarcastically, that it was the one who did it, so ask them, if they can speak. The people were confronted with their own foolishness, momentarily reflecting inwardly, before reverting to their old ways and insisting the idols do not speak, to which Ibrahim replied, asking why then they worship what neither benefits nor harms them.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:57-67
references.gist: Ibrahim breaks the idols except the biggest, is confronted, and turns their own reasoning against them.

chapters.heading: Into the Fire
chapters.narrative: Angered and humiliated, the people called for Ibrahim to be burned in defense of their gods. They built a fire and threw him into it. Allah commanded the fire directly: fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim. Their plot to destroy him instead left them as the losers, unable to harm him at all.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:68-70
references.gist: The people throw Ibrahim into the fire; Allah commands the fire to be cool and safe for him, and his enemies are the losers.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:24
references.gist: A parallel, shorter statement: they wanted to burn him but Allah saved him; there are signs in this for believers.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:97-98
references.gist: They said to build a structure for him and cast him into the blazing fire, but their plan was turned into the lowest outcome.

chapters.heading: Debating the King
chapters.narrative: A king who had grown arrogant because of the power he held argued with Ibrahim about his Lord. Ibrahim said his Lord is the one who gives life and causes death. The king claimed he too could give life and cause death, apparently by pardoning a condemned man and executing another. Ibrahim then said Allah brings the sun from the east, so let the king bring it from the west. The disbelieving king was left stunned and speechless, unable to answer.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:258
references.gist: Ibrahim's debate with an unnamed king who claimed power over life, death, and the natural order; the king is left dumbfounded.

chapters.heading: Guests With Two Messages
chapters.narrative: Messengers, angels in human form, came to Ibrahim with a greeting of peace. He hurried to bring them a roasted calf, but when he saw their hands did not reach for the food, he grew uneasy. They told him not to fear, they had been sent also to the people of Lut. His wife, standing nearby, laughed in astonishment, and they gave her glad tidings of a son, Ishaq, and after him Ya'qub, despite her old age. When his fear had passed, Ibrahim began to plead on behalf of Lut's people, though the matter had already been decided; the same guests then went on toward Lut with news of the coming destruction of his people.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:69-76
references.gist: The angelic guests bring Ibrahim news of Ishaq's birth, then reveal they are sent to destroy the people of Lut; Ibrahim pleads on Lut's behalf.

references.label: Surah Adh-Dhariyat 51:24-34
references.gist: Parallel account of the honored guests, the calf, the glad tidings of a knowledgeable son, and their mission against a criminal people.

references.label: Surah Al-Hijr 15:51-56
references.gist: Another telling of the same guests, Ibrahim's fear, and the glad tidings, with Ibrahim asking not to be among the despairing.

chapters.heading: Hajar and Isma'il in the Valley of Makkah
chapters.narrative: According to the long narration of Ibn Abbas in Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibrahim brought Hajar and their infant son Isma'il to a barren place near where the Ka'ba would stand, with no people and no water, leaving them with only a bag of dates and a small waterskin before returning home. When the water ran out and the infant grew distressed, Hajar ran between the hills of Safa and Marwa seven times searching for help, the origin, the hadith states, of the ritual walking between the two hills performed in Hajj and Umrah to this day. On her final return to Marwa she heard a sound; an angel struck the ground and water sprang forth at the spot that became the well of Zamzam. Hajar built a basin around it, and the flowing water later drew the tribe of Jurhum to settle there, among whom Isma'il grew up and eventually married.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3364
references.gist: Ibn Abbas's long narration: Ibrahim leaves Hajar and infant Isma'il near the future site of the Ka'ba; Hajar's search between Safa and Marwa; the angel opens the spring of Zamzam.

chapters.heading: Raising the House
chapters.narrative: Years later Ibrahim returned to visit his son, whom he found mending arrows near the well. He told Isma'il that Allah had commanded him to build a house there, and Isma'il agreed to help. Together they raised the foundations, with Isma'il carrying the stones and Ibrahim building, both of them praying: our Lord, accept this from us, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. As the walls grew too high for Ibrahim to reach, he stood on a stone, which became known as Maqam Ibrahim, while Isma'il continued handing him stones, until the House was completed.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:127
references.gist: Ibrahim and Isma'il raise the foundations of the House, praying for Allah to accept their work.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3365
references.gist: Ibrahim finds Isma'il mending arrows, tells him of the command to build the House; together they raise it, Ibrahim standing on the stone of the Maqam as the walls grow high.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:125
references.gist: Commands believers to take from the standing place (Maqam) of Ibrahim a place of prayer, naming the site directly.

chapters.heading: The Dream of Sacrifice
chapters.narrative: When his son was old enough to work alongside him, Ibrahim told him he had seen in a dream that he must sacrifice him, and asked his view. The son answered that his father should do as he was commanded, and that he would be found, God willing, among the patient. When both had submitted to Allah's will and Ibrahim had laid him down, Allah called out that Ibrahim had already fulfilled the vision, and ransomed the son with a great sacrifice instead, leaving Ibrahim's example to be remembered by later generations. The Quran does not name which son this was; it says only that Ibrahim was given the news of a forbearing boy before this test, and only afterward, in verses immediately following, gives the separate glad tidings of Ishaq as a prophet. Because of that ordering, and because the Quran elsewhere says Isma'il fulfilled what he promised regarding himself, many scholars hold it was Isma'il, though a substantial classical position holds it was Ishaq; the Quran itself does not settle the question by name.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:99-111
references.gist: Ibrahim's dream, his son's willing submission, and Allah's ransom of him with a great sacrifice; the son is not named.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:112-113
references.gist: Immediately after the sacrifice narrative, Ishaq is separately announced as a prophet among the righteous, textual grounds cited by those who read the earlier, unnamed son as Isma'il.

chapters.heading: A Prayer for Makkah and His Line
chapters.narrative: Ibrahim prayed that Makkah be made a city of security, and that he and his children be kept safe from idol worship, acknowledging that these idols had misled many. He described settling some of his offspring in this barren valley by the Sacred House so that they might establish prayer, asking Allah to incline people's hearts toward them and provide them with fruits. He gave praise for being granted Isma'il and Ishaq in his old age, and asked that he and his descendants remain steadfast in prayer, closing with a request for forgiveness for himself, his parents, and the believers on the Day of Reckoning.

references.label: Surah Ibrahim 14:35-41
references.gist: Ibrahim's prayer for the security of Makkah, protection from idolatry for himself and his descendants, and for steadfastness in prayer across generations.

name: Isma'il (AS)
lineage: A direct son of Ibrahim (AS), born to Hajar.
summary: The elder son of Ibrahim (AS), born to Hajar. Most scholars hold he was the son Ibrahim was commanded in a vision to sacrifice, and who willingly submitted to it before Allah replaced the sacrifice with a ram. He later helped his father build the Kaaba and is the ancestor, through many generations, of Muhammad (SAW).

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:100-113
references.gist: Covers the son's willing submission to being sacrificed and Allah's ransom of him with a great sacrifice, without naming which son.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:124-127
references.gist: Covers Ibrahim and Isma'il raising the foundations of the House together.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3364
references.gist: Ibn Abbas's long narration in which Isma'il grows up near the Zamzam spring and later helps build the Ka'ba.

tale.intro: Much of Isma'il's early life, being left with his mother Hajar near the future site of the Ka'ba, the spring of Zamzam, and building the House with his father, is told fully in Ibrahim's tale; see that entry for those events. This tale covers what the Quran attributes to Isma'il in his own right.

chapters.heading: The Son Who Submitted
chapters.narrative: When his father told him of the dream commanding a sacrifice, the son's response was immediate submission: he told his father to carry out what he was commanded, and that he would be found patient. Both father and son submitted to the command before Allah ransomed the son with a sacrifice instead. As noted in Ibrahim's tale, the Quran does not name this son directly, the passage simply calls him a forbearing boy given as good news before the later, separately named announcement of Ishaq's birth as a prophet. Many scholars, reading that sequence together with the verse below about Isma'il's own truthfulness to his promise, hold that this was Isma'il, while a real body of classical opinion holds it was Ishaq. The matter is not settled by the Quran's own wording.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:100-107
references.gist: The son's calm submission to being sacrificed, and Allah's ransom of him with a great sacrifice.

chapters.heading: True to His Promise
chapters.narrative: The Quran separately praises Isma'il by name as someone who was true to what he promised, and describes him as a messenger and a prophet who used to instruct his family to pray and to give charity, and with whom his Lord was pleased.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:54-55
references.gist: Isma'il is named directly and praised as true to his promise, a messenger and prophet who commanded his family to pray and give charity.

name: Ishaq (AS)
lineage: A direct son of Ibrahim (AS), born to Sarah in her old age.
summary: The son of Ibrahim (AS) and Sarah, born to them in old age as glad tidings brought by angels, who also foretold that his own son would be Ya'qub. The Quran names him a prophet and one of the righteous.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:71-73
references.gist: Covers the angelic guests announcing Ishaq's birth to Ibrahim and Sarah in their old age.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:112-113
references.gist: Announces Ishaq by name as a prophet and one of the righteous.

tale.intro: Ishaq's birth to Ibrahim and Sarah in their old age, announced by the angelic guests, is told in Ibrahim's tale. The Quran's material specifically about Ishaq himself, apart from his father's story, is brief, and this entry stays honest about that scope rather than padding it out.

chapters.heading: A Prophet Among the Righteous
chapters.narrative: Directly after the account of Ibrahim's sacrifice trial, the Quran gives a separate announcement: glad tidings of Ishaq, a prophet, one of the righteous. Allah blessed both Ibrahim and Ishaq, though among their descendants some would be doers of good and others clearly unjust to themselves.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:112-113
references.gist: Ishaq is announced by name as a prophet and one of the righteous, with a blessing on him and his father, and a note that his descendants would include both the righteous and the unjust.

chapters.heading: Placed Among a Line of Prophets
chapters.narrative: Elsewhere the Quran lists Ishaq alongside Ibrahim and Ya'qub as men Allah guided, and states that Allah placed prophethood and scripture among Ibrahim's descendants through this line, rewarding him with good in this world and counting him, in the next, among the righteous.

references.label: Surah Al-An'am 6:84-86
references.gist: Ishaq listed with Ya'qub and other prophets as among those Allah guided from Ibrahim's line.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:27
references.gist: Allah gave Ibrahim Ishaq and Ya'qub, and placed prophethood and scripture among his descendants.

name: Ya'qub (AS)
lineage: A direct son of Ishaq (AS).
summary: The son of Ishaq (AS) and grandson of Ibrahim (AS), father of twelve sons who became the tribes of Bani Isra'il. His story of grief over the loss of Yusuf and enduring patience is told alongside his son's throughout Surah Yusuf.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:4-6
references.gist: Covers Yusuf's dream and Ya'qub's warning not to tell his brothers.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:84-87
references.gist: Covers Ya'qub's grief and blindness over the loss of Yusuf, and his continued patience.

tale.intro: Ya'qub's story is woven through Surah Yusuf, where the fuller narrative of his son Yusuf is told in detail; see Yusuf's tale for that account. This entry focuses on what the Quran shows specifically from Ya'qub's own perspective: his grief, his patience, and his final words to his sons.

chapters.heading: Beautiful Patience
chapters.narrative: When his sons returned having lost Yusuf and brought a false story to explain it, Ya'qub did not believe them but responded that patience is most fitting, and Allah is the one sought for help against what they described. Later, when his sons returned a second time grieving the loss of another brother, Ya'qub used the same words again: beautiful patience. He told them he only complained of his suffering and grief to Allah, and that he knew from Allah what they did not know.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:18
references.gist: Ya'qub's response of beautiful patience on first hearing the brothers' false account of Yusuf's disappearance.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:83
references.gist: Ya'qub repeats the same phrase of beautiful patience after losing another son, and says he complains only to Allah.

chapters.heading: Grief, Blindness, and Sight Restored
chapters.narrative: Ya'qub's continued grief and suppressed sorrow over Yusuf caused his eyes to turn white, the Quran's way of describing that he lost his sight. He told his sons he only complained of his anguish to Allah, and that he knew of Allah's mercy in ways they did not, even rebuking them gently for despairing. Later, when Yusuf, by then revealed and reunited with his family, sent his shirt ahead with instructions to place it over his father's face, Ya'qub's sight was restored the moment it touched him, and he told those around him that he had always known from Allah what they did not know.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:84-87
references.gist: Ya'qub's eyes turn white from grief; he tells his sons he complains only to Allah and knows things they do not.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:93-96
references.gist: Yusuf's shirt is sent ahead and placed on Ya'qub's face, restoring his sight.

chapters.heading: His Final Instruction
chapters.narrative: As death approached him, Ya'qub gathered his sons and asked what they would worship after he was gone. They answered that they would worship his God, the God of his forefathers Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and that they submitted to Him alone.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:132-133
references.gist: Ya'qub, near death, asks his sons what they will worship after him; they affirm worship of the one God of their forefathers.

name: Shu'ayb (AS)
lineage: Not established as a descendant of any prophet in this tree; the Quran and hadith do not fix his lineage, so no connecting line is shown.
summary: Known for his eloquence, Shu'ayb was sent to the people of Madyan, calling them to worship Allah alone and to stop cheating people by shortchanging weights and measures. When they rejected him, they were seized by a violent blast and left fallen lifeless in their homes.

placementNote.text: Shu'ayb is placed here, after Lut, following the order the Quran itself tells these destroyed-people accounts in (Nuh, then 'Aad, then Thamud, then Lut, then Madyan). Unlike Hud and Salih, though, no verse states Madyan succeeded an earlier people, so this row is the account's narrative order, not a textually fixed chronology.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:59-93
references.gist: Tells Nuh, Hud/'Aad, Salih/Thamud, Lut, and Shu'ayb/Madyan in that sequence, one after another.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:85-93
references.gist: Covers Shu'ayb's warning to Madyan about dishonest measure and weight, and their subsequent destruction.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:84-95
references.gist: Covers Shu'ayb's call to Madyan and the blast that struck them after they rejected him.

tale.intro: Shu'ayb (AS) was sent to the people of Madyan, who are also addressed in the Quran as the companions of the wood (Ashab al-Aykah); classical commentary generally treats these as either the same community or closely related, addressed by the same warnings.

chapters.heading: Sent to Madyan
chapters.narrative: Shu'ayb was sent as a messenger to his people of Madyan. He told them to worship Allah alone, and warned them specifically against giving less than due in measure and weight, and against sitting along every path threatening travelers and turning people away from the way of Allah, recalling how Allah had multiplied them in number. He called them to give full measure and full weight in justice, and not to deprive people of what was rightfully theirs or spread corruption in the land.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:85-93
references.gist: Shu'ayb warns Madyan against cheating in measure and weight, threatening travelers on the road, and corruption, and calls them to Allah alone.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:84-95
references.gist: Parallel account of Shu'ayb's warning to Madyan about honest measure and weight and not withholding people's due.

chapters.heading: The Same Warning to the Companions of the Wood
chapters.narrative: In another telling, addressed to the companions of the wood, Shu'ayb again calls his people to fear Allah and be conscious of Him, to give full measure without shortchanging, to weigh with an even scale, not to defraud people of their due, and not to spread corruption in the land, invoking the same standard of honest dealing found in the account addressed to Madyan.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:176-191
references.gist: Shu'ayb warns the companions of the wood about full measure, honest weighing, and corruption, in language mirroring his warning to Madyan.

references.label: Surah Al-Ankabut 29:36-37
references.gist: A brief account: Shu'ayb calls Madyan to worship Allah alone and beware the Last Day, and warns against causing corruption.

chapters.heading: Rejection and Destruction
chapters.narrative: Shu'ayb's people mocked him, questioning whether his prayer commanded him to make them abandon what their forefathers worshipped or stop them from doing as they wished with their wealth, and the arrogant among them threatened to expel him and his followers from their town unless they returned to their old ways. In the accounts addressed to Madyan, a violent earthquake seized them, leaving them fallen lifeless in their homes; in the account addressed to the companions of the wood, their punishment came differently, described as the punishment of the day of the shadow, a scourge the Quran itself does not describe in further detail, following a period of overshadowing heat. Shu'ayb turned away from his destroyed people, telling them he had conveyed his Lord's message and advised them sincerely.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:88-93
references.gist: The arrogant leaders threaten to expel Shu'ayb and the believers; an earthquake seizes the people, and Shu'ayb laments over them afterward.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:94
references.gist: A mighty blast (the shout) seizes Madyan, and they are left fallen lifeless in their homes.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:189
references.gist: The companions of the wood are seized by the punishment of the day of the overshadowing shadow, described as the punishment of a terrible day.

name: Yusuf (AS)
lineage: A direct son of Ya'qub (AS).
summary: The son of Ya'qub (AS), thrown into a well by his jealous brothers and sold into slavery in Egypt. After enduring false accusation and imprisonment, he rose to a position of authority in Egypt and, after years apart, was reunited with and forgave his family. The Prophet Muhammad (SAW) described him as 'the noble one, son of the noble one, son of the noble one, son of the noble one: Yusuf, son of Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim.'

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:1-111
references.gist: The full account of Yusuf: his dream, being sold into slavery, the temptation in Egypt, prison, his rise to authority, and reunion with his family.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3353
references.gist: The Prophet describes Yusuf as the noble son of the noble son of the noble son of the noble son, tracing his line back through Ya'qub, Ishaq, and Ibrahim.

tale.intro: The story of Yusuf occupies nearly the whole of Surah Yusuf (Surah 12), told as one continuous, unusually detailed narrative; the Quran itself calls it the best of stories.

chapters.heading: The Dream
chapters.narrative: As a boy, Yusuf told his father Ya'qub that he had seen eleven stars, and the sun and the moon, prostrating to him. Ya'qub, recognizing what this meant, warned him gently not to tell his brothers, fearing they would plot against him out of envy, and told him Allah would choose him and teach him the interpretation of narratives, completing His favor upon him and his family as He had upon Ibrahim and Ishaq before him.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:4-6
references.gist: Yusuf's dream of eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrating to him; Ya'qub's warning and recognition of what it meant.

chapters.heading: The Well and the Caravan
chapters.narrative: Yusuf's brothers grew jealous, seeing that he and his younger brother were more beloved to their father, and plotted to kill him or cast him out to some land so their father's attention would turn to them alone. One brother suggested instead throwing him into the bottom of a well, where travelers might pick him up. They asked their father to let Yusuf go out with them, promising to protect him, then threw him into the well and returned to their father with his shirt stained in false blood, claiming a wolf had eaten him, though Ya'qub did not believe them and met it with patience. A caravan later stopped at the well, drew Yusuf up, and sold him for a low price in Egypt, where a man described as al-Aziz bought him and told his wife to make his stay honorable.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:7-20
references.gist: The brothers' jealousy and plot, casting Yusuf into a well, the false story to their father, and Yusuf being found and sold into slavery in Egypt.

chapters.heading: Tested in the House of al-Aziz
chapters.narrative: As Yusuf grew up in the household, given wisdom and knowledge by Allah, the wife of al-Aziz attempted to seduce him, locking the doors and inviting him. Yusuf refused, saying he sought refuge in Allah, and that his master had treated him honorably, wrongdoers do not prosper. As they both raced to the door, she tore his shirt from behind. When al-Aziz found them, she accused Yusuf, but a witness from her own household reasoned that if the shirt was torn from behind, she was lying and he was truthful; al-Aziz recognized the truth of the matter from the direction of the tear and told her to seek forgiveness for her sin.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:21-29
references.gist: Yusuf's upbringing in al-Aziz's house, the wife's attempted seduction, his refusal, and the torn shirt proving his innocence.

chapters.heading: The Women of the City, and Prison Chosen Over Sin
chapters.narrative: Word of the incident spread, and women of the city gossiped about al-Aziz's wife. She invited them to a gathering, gave each a knife, and had Yusuf enter; astonished by his beauty, the women cut their own hands without noticing. She admitted she had tried to seduce him and that he had refused, adding that if he did not do as she commanded he would be imprisoned. Yusuf prayed that prison was more beloved to him than what they called him to, and asked Allah to turn their plotting away from him. His prayer was answered, and after these signs were seen, they nonetheless decided to imprison him for a time.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:30-35
references.gist: The women of the city, the gathering where they cut their hands in astonishment, al-Aziz's wife's admission, and Yusuf's prayer preferring prison to sin.

chapters.heading: Interpreting Dreams in Prison
chapters.narrative: In prison, two young men had dreams they asked Yusuf to interpret, one that he was pressing wine, the other that he carried bread on his head that birds were eating from. Before answering, Yusuf spoke to them of the oneness of Allah and rejected the way of his ancestors' polytheism, then told them one would return to serving his master's drink, while the other would be crucified and birds would eat from his head. He asked the one he expected to be freed to mention him to his master, but the man forgot for some years.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:36-42
references.gist: Yusuf interprets the dreams of his two fellow prisoners and asks the one to be freed to remember him, though the man forgets.

chapters.heading: The King's Dream and Vindication
