chapters.narrative: Years later the king of Egypt saw seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and seven dry ones, and sought an interpretation. The former prisoner, now remembering Yusuf, brought his question to him in prison. Yusuf explained that seven years of abundant harvest would be followed by seven years of famine, advising that grain be stored during the good years and one year set aside for relief. When the king asked for him to be brought out, Yusuf insisted first that the king question the women who had cut their hands, so the truth of his innocence would be clear; they, including al-Aziz's wife, testified that he was truthful and had committed no wrong. Yusuf was then brought before the king and placed in a position of trust.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:43-49
references.gist: The king's dream of seven fat and lean cows and Yusuf's interpretation of coming years of plenty and famine.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:50-53
references.gist: Yusuf asks that the women be questioned first; they testify to his innocence, exonerating him before he leaves prison.

chapters.heading: Placed Over the Treasuries of Egypt
chapters.narrative: Yusuf asked to be placed in charge of the storehouses of the land, describing himself as a trustworthy guardian with knowledge suited to the task. He was established with authority in the land, settling wherever he wished, with Allah's mercy reaching whoever He willed among the doers of good.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:54-57
references.gist: Yusuf is appointed over Egypt's storehouses and established with authority in the land.

chapters.heading: The Brothers Return, and the Planted Cup
chapters.narrative: When famine reached Ya'qub's family, his sons came to Egypt for provisions and stood before Yusuf without recognizing him. He gave them full measure and asked them to bring their youngest brother next time, holding one brother back as a guarantee. When they returned with Benjamin, Yusuf revealed himself privately to him alone, then had a drinking cup placed in Benjamin's bag before announcing a theft and searching their belongings. The cup was found, and by the law they themselves had agreed to, Benjamin was kept back in Egypt, to the brothers' distress, since they had sworn to their father to bring him home safely.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:58-79
references.gist: The brothers come to Egypt for grain, are told to bring Benjamin, Yusuf reveals himself privately to Benjamin, and the planted cup leads to Benjamin being kept in Egypt.

chapters.heading: The Reveal
chapters.narrative: The brothers debated staying rather than facing their father again, and the eldest resolved not to leave Egypt until his father permitted it or Allah judged for him. Ya'qub, hearing what had happened, again responded with beautiful patience, grieving so deeply for both sons that his eyes turned white. When the brothers eventually returned to Yusuf pleading for mercy and more provisions, Yusuf finally asked them if they remembered what they had done to Yusuf and his brother in their ignorance. Realizing who stood before them, they were astonished; Yusuf told them there was no blame upon them that day, that Allah would forgive them, and sent his shirt for them to carry back to restore their father's sight.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:80-93
references.gist: The brothers' distress, Ya'qub's continued grief, and Yusuf's eventual revelation of his identity and forgiveness of his brothers.

chapters.heading: Reunion and Fulfilled Vision
chapters.narrative: When the caravan departed Egypt, Ya'qub, though far away, said he could sense the scent of Yusuf. The shirt reached him and restored his sight, and the family was reunited in Egypt. Yusuf raised his parents to the highest seat, and they all fell down in prostration before him, fulfilling the dream of his childhood. He told his father this was the interpretation of that old vision, and turned to Allah in gratitude, acknowledging that He had been good to him, brought him out of prison, and brought his family from the desert after Shaytan had caused strife between him and his brothers. Yusuf then prayed that Allah cause him to die in submission to Him and join him with the righteous.

references.label: Surah Yusuf 12:94-101
references.gist: Ya'qub senses Yusuf's presence and his sight is restored; the family reunites in Egypt, his parents and brothers prostrate before him, fulfilling his childhood dream, and Yusuf offers a prayer of gratitude.

name: Ayyub (AS)
lineage: A descendant of Ishaq (AS), many generations later; the exact chain of names is not given in the Quran and differs between classical sources.
summary: Tried with the loss of his wealth, children, and health, Ayyub bore his suffering with exemplary patience, calling on Allah only after years of hardship: 'Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.' Allah answered him, telling him to strike the ground so that a cool spring burst forth, and restored his health, family, and wealth.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:83-84
references.gist: Covers Ayyub's prayer in his affliction and Allah's restoration of his health and family.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:41-44
references.gist: Covers Ayyub's distress, the spring of water for his relief, and the bundle of grass by which he fulfilled his oath.

tale.intro: Ayyub is held up in the Quran as the model of patient endurance through affliction, and of Allah's mercy in restoring what was lost.

chapters.heading: Affliction and the Prayer
chapters.narrative: Ayyub was tested with severe illness and loss, touched, as the Quran puts it, with hardship and torment. In his distress, he called upon his Lord, saying adversity had touched him, and Allah was the Most Merciful of the merciful.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:83
references.gist: Ayyub's prayer in distress: adversity has touched him, and Allah is the Most Merciful of the merciful.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:41
references.gist: Ayyub calls on his Lord, afflicted with distress and torment.

chapters.heading: Restoration and Double Blessing
chapters.narrative: Allah responded to Ayyub's prayer and removed the harm afflicting him. He was told to strike the ground with his foot, and a spring of cool water gushed forth for him to wash in and drink, relieving his suffering. Allah then restored his family to him, granting others like them alongside them, as a mercy from Him and a reminder to those who serve Him. The Quran commends Ayyub as an excellent servant, one who constantly turned back to his Lord.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:84
references.gist: Allah removes Ayyub's affliction and restores his family, doubling it, as a mercy and a reminder.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:42-44
references.gist: Ayyub is told to strike the ground for a healing spring, and his family and strength are restored.

chapters.heading: The Bundle of Grass and the Oath
chapters.narrative: Ayyub had sworn an oath; the Quran does not state here what it concerned or against whom. So that he might fulfill it without breaking it, he was instructed to take in his hand a bundle of grass and strike with it, rather than break his oath. In this way he honored his vow while causing no real harm. The Quran affirms of him that he was found patient, an excellent servant, one repeatedly turning back to Allah.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:44
references.gist: Ayyub is told to strike with a bundle of grass to fulfill his oath without breaking it; he is praised as patient and excellent.

name: Musa (AS)
lineage: A descendant of Ishaq (AS), many generations later.
summary: Spoken to directly by Allah at the burning bush and sent to Pharaoh to free the Children of Israel. He was given the Torah and supported with signs, including his staff, and Allah saved him and drowned Pharaoh's army when they pursued him to the sea.

provenDates.label: Agreed to serve his father-in-law 8 years, or 10 if completed, in exchange for marriage

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:27
references.gist: The old man of Madyan offers Musa marriage in exchange for eight years of service, or ten if he completes them.

provenDates.label: His people barred from the holy land, left to wander 40 years

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:26
references.gist: Allah forbids the holy land to them for forty years, during which they wander the land, as punishment for refusing to enter it.

family.name: Not named in the Quran or in any authentic hadith
family.note: Quran 28:22-28 describes a righteous elderly man in Madyan whose daughter Musa marries, without naming or identifying him (that passage is this entry's reference); a dedicated search across the major hadith collections found no authentic hadith addressing his identity either.

family.name: Not named in the Quran or any confirmed Islamic source
family.note: Quran 28:27 mentions one of the two daughters is given to Musa in marriage, without naming her (that verse is this entry's reference); a dedicated search across the major hadith collections found no Quran or hadith basis for a name at all.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:9-98
references.gist: Covers the burning bush and call to prophethood, the confrontation with Pharaoh, the magicians, and the Golden Calf.

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:1-43
references.gist: Covers Musa's birth and being placed in the river, his flight to Madyan, his marriage there, and his calling as a messenger.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3397
references.gist: The Prophet describes fasting on the Day of Ashura in commemoration of Musa and the Israelites' deliverance from Pharaoh at the sea.

tale.intro: Musa's story spans more of the Quran than that of any other prophet, told piece by piece across many surahs, from his infancy under Pharaoh's tyranny to a mysterious encounter with a righteous servant in the wilderness years later.

chapters.heading: The Child in the River
chapters.narrative: Musa was born into danger. Fearing for her infant, his mother was inspired by Allah: if she feared for him, she should cast him into a chest and set it upon the river, and Allah would return him to her and make him one of His messengers. The river carried the chest to the household of Pharaoh himself, an enemy to Allah and to him. Musa's sister, sent to follow the chest from a distance, saw where it came to rest, and seeing the household's need for a nurse, recommended a woman for the task. So Musa was restored to his own mother's arms, that she might be comforted and not grieve.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:38-40
references.gist: Allah recalls inspiring Musa's mother to cast him into the river; he was raised under Allah's watch.

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:7-13
references.gist: Musa's mother casts him into the river; his sister follows; he is restored to his mother to nurse him.

chapters.heading: The Killing and the Flight
chapters.narrative: Grown to maturity, Musa was given judgment and knowledge by Allah. Entering the city while its people were unaware, he found two men fighting, one of his own people, one of Pharaoh's. When the Israelite cried out for his help, Musa struck the Egyptian with his fist, and the blow killed him. Recognizing this as wrong, he sought his Lord's forgiveness, and was forgiven. The next day, seeing the same Israelite in another quarrel and being called on again, Musa rebuked him, and the man, frightened Musa meant to strike him too, exposed that he had killed a man. A stranger then ran from the far side of the city to warn Musa that the chiefs were plotting to kill him, and Musa fled in fear, praying for deliverance from the wrongdoers.

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:14-21
references.gist: Musa strikes and kills an Egyptian by accident, seeks forgiveness, and flees the city after being warned of a plot.

chapters.heading: Marriage in Madyan
chapters.narrative: Musa arrived at the well of Madyan to find shepherds watering their flocks, and set apart from them, two women holding back their own. Asked why, they explained they could not go in among the men, and waited because their father was very old. Musa watered the flocks for them and withdrew to the shade, praying for whatever good Allah might send him. One of the women, sent by her father, invited Musa to the household to be rewarded. There, the father, an old man the Quran does not name, offered Musa marriage to one of his two daughters, on condition he work for him eight years, or ten if he chose to complete them as a favor, and Musa agreed.

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:22-28
references.gist: Musa waters the two women's flocks in Madyan, is invited home, and agrees to work eight to ten years for marriage to one daughter.

chapters.heading: The Burning Bush and the Call
chapters.narrative: Travelling on with his family, Musa saw a fire in the distance and went toward it, hoping for a burning brand or guidance. At the fire, in the blessed valley of Tuwa, he was addressed directly and told to remove his sandals, for he was in the sacred valley. Allah declared His oneness and commanded him to worship Him and establish prayer. Asked what was in his right hand, Musa answered it was his staff; told to cast it down, it became a moving serpent, then, taken back without fear, it returned to being a staff. He was told to put his hand into his cloak and draw it out; it emerged shining white, without any disease, a second sign. Allah told him he had been chosen and appointed a prophet, commanded to go to Pharaoh, who had transgressed all bounds. Musa asked that his chest be expanded, his task eased, the knot loosened from his tongue so people would understand him, and that his brother Harun be appointed as a helper and partner in his mission, a prayer that was granted.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:9-24
references.gist: The fire, the command to remove sandals, the call to prophethood, and the two signs of the staff and the white hand.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:7-12
references.gist: Parallel account of the fire and the call, with the staff and hand as signs to Pharaoh's people.

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:29-35
references.gist: Parallel account; Musa asks for Harun to be sent with him as support.

chapters.heading: Before Pharaoh
chapters.narrative: Musa and Harun were commanded to go to Pharaoh together and to speak to him gently, that he might be reminded or come to fear Allah. They told him they were messengers of the Lord of the worlds, sent to demand the release of the Children of Israel. Pharaoh questioned Musa's identity, reminding him he had been raised in his household and had killed a man; Musa acknowledged the act as an error, while affirming Allah's mercy and his own mission. Pharaoh dismissed the message, accused the brothers of sorcery meant to drive the Egyptians from their land, and demanded a sign.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:42-56
references.gist: Musa and Harun sent to Pharaoh with gentle speech; Pharaoh demands to know who their Lord is.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:10-51
references.gist: Musa confronts Pharaoh, recounts the killing, and Pharaoh accuses him of sorcery.

chapters.heading: The Contest with the Magicians
chapters.narrative: Pharaoh summoned the most skilled magicians in the land, promising them reward and status if they defeated Musa. Before a gathered crowd, the magicians threw down their ropes and staffs, which through sorcery appeared to move like snakes, striking the onlookers with awe. Musa, told not to fear, threw down his own staff, and it swallowed up what they had fabricated. Recognizing this was no trick, the magicians fell down in prostration, declaring belief in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun. Pharaoh, enraged, accused them of conspiring with Musa and threatened to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them, but the magicians, unmoved, said they would return to their Lord regardless, asking only for patience and to die in submission to Him.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:103-126
references.gist: The magicians are summoned, the contest occurs, and they fall in prostration and believe.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:56-73
references.gist: Parallel account of the contest and the magicians' sudden belief despite Pharaoh's threats.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:38-51
references.gist: Parallel account; the magicians declare belief in the Lord of Musa and Harun.

chapters.heading: The Plagues
chapters.narrative: Allah afflicted Pharaoh's people with years of drought and shortage of crops as a reminder, but they remained arrogant, blaming any hardship on Musa and his people. Then came a succession of distinct afflictions: a flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood. Each time a plague struck, Pharaoh's people pleaded with Musa that if it were lifted they would believe and let the Israelites go, and each time it was lifted, they broke their word.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:130-135
references.gist: Drought, then the flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood strike Pharaoh's people; they repeatedly break their promises.

chapters.heading: The Exodus and the Sea
chapters.narrative: Musa was commanded to lead the Children of Israel out of Egypt by night, and Pharaoh sent heralds to gather his forces in pursuit. When the two groups came within sight of each other, the Israelites, trapped by the sea, feared being overtaken. Musa reassured them his Lord was with him. Commanded to strike the sea with his staff, he did, and it parted, each part standing like a great mountain, opening a dry path through which the Israelites crossed. Pharaoh and his army followed into the sea; once the Israelites had safely crossed, the waters closed over Pharaoh and his army, drowning them all while the Israelites looked on.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:77-79
references.gist: Musa strikes the sea with his staff on Allah's command, opening a dry path; Pharaoh's army is engulfed.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:52-68
references.gist: The sea parts into mountain-like sections; Pharaoh's army drowns as the Israelites cross safely.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:50
references.gist: Allah recalls parting the sea and saving the Israelites while drowning Pharaoh's people before their eyes.

chapters.heading: Mount Sinai and the Tablets
chapters.narrative: Allah appointed for Musa a term of thirty nights, completed with ten more, forty nights in all at Mount Sinai. Before leaving, Musa told Harun to take his place among the people, act rightly, and not follow the way of those who cause corruption. When Musa's Lord spoke to him, he asked to see Him, and was told he could not bear it; Allah manifested His glory to the mountain instead, and it crumbled to dust, at which Musa fell unconscious. On recovering, he declared Allah's transcendence and turned to Him in repentance. Allah then wrote for him upon the Tablets instruction and explanation for all things, commanding him to hold fast to them and command his people to take the best of it.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:142-145
references.gist: The forty nights at Sinai, Musa's request to see Allah, the mountain's crumbling, and the giving of the Tablets.

chapters.heading: The Golden Calf
chapters.narrative: In Musa's absence, the Israelites, using ornaments they possessed, made a calf that produced a lowing sound, and took to worshipping it, though it neither spoke to them nor guided them to any way. Allah asked Musa why he had hurried ahead of his people; Musa explained he hastened to please his Lord, and then learned his people had gone astray in his absence, led by a man identified as al-Samiri. Returning in anger and grief, Musa threw down the Tablets and seized his brother Harun by the head, demanding to know why he had not stopped them. Harun explained he had tried to warn them but was overpowered, fearing that forceful action would split the community and that Musa would then blame him for causing division. Musa confronted al-Samiri, who admitted responsibility; Musa then had the calf burned and its remains scattered into the sea, and prayed for forgiveness for himself and his brother.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:148-155
references.gist: The Israelites worship the calf; Musa's anger, his seizing of Harun, and his prayer for forgiveness.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:83-98
references.gist: Musa learns of the calf and al-Samiri's role, confronts him, and destroys the calf.

chapters.heading: Manna and Quails
chapters.narrative: As the Israelites wandered, Allah shaded them with clouds and sent down manna and quails, telling them to eat from the good things provided for them.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:57
references.gist: Allah shades the Israelites with clouds and provides manna and quails in the wilderness.

chapters.heading: Musa and the Righteous Servant
chapters.narrative: Musa told his young companion he would not stop until he reached the junction of the two seas, even if it took him a long time. There they found one of Allah's servants, a righteous man given mercy and knowledge from Allah, left unnamed throughout this passage, and Musa asked to follow him to learn some of the right guidance he had been taught. The man warned Musa he would not be able to bear patiently with what he would witness, but agreed to let him accompany him on condition Musa not question him until he himself explained. Three times the man did something that alarmed Musa, and three times Musa's promise of patience broke: he scuttled a boat belonging to poor workers at sea; he killed a young boy; and in a town that had refused them hospitality, he repaired a collapsing wall without payment. After the third breach, he explained: the boat was damaged to save it from a king forcibly seizing every good vessel; the boy was killed because his righteous believing parents would have been overwhelmed by his growing into transgression, and Allah intended to give them one better in purity and closer in mercy; and the wall was restored because beneath it lay treasure belonging to two orphan boys whose father had been righteous, meant for them to recover once they came of age, as a mercy from their Lord. He told Musa this was not done upon his own command. The Quran leaves this servant unnamed, but an authenticated hadith of the Prophet Muhammad, retelling this same journey, identifies him as al-Khidr.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:60-82
references.gist: Musa follows an unnamed righteous servant of Allah through three trials of patience, each later explained.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3401
references.gist: The Prophet Muhammad narrates this same journey and identifies the unnamed servant as al-Khidr.

name: Harun (AS)
lineage: A direct brother of Musa (AS), sharing the same father and mother; like Musa, a descendant of Ibrahim (AS) through his son Ishaq (AS), many generations later.
summary: The elder brother of Musa (AS), granted prophethood alongside him in answer to Musa's prayer for a helper who was more eloquent in speech. He supported Musa throughout the confrontation with Pharaoh and the years in the wilderness that followed.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:29-36
references.gist: Musa's prayer for Harun to be appointed his helper and partner in the prophetic mission.

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:34-35
references.gist: Musa asks for Harun to be sent with him as support before Pharaoh, and Allah grants the request.

tale.intro: Harun's story runs alongside his brother Musa's for most of the Quran; the fuller shared narrative, the mission to Pharaoh, the plagues, the Exodus, is told in Musa's tale. This entry focuses on what is distinctly Harun's own.

chapters.heading: Granted as Musa's Helper
chapters.narrative: When Musa was commissioned as a prophet, he prayed that his brother Harun be made a partner in his task, to increase his strength through him, concerned about his own difficulty of speech before Pharaoh's court and wanting someone to share and support his message. Allah granted the request. Elsewhere the Quran confirms that Musa was given the Scripture and Harun was appointed alongside him as a helper.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:29-36
references.gist: Musa prays for Harun to be appointed his minister and partner in the mission; the request is granted.

references.label: Surah Al-Furqan 25:35
references.gist: Musa was given the Scripture and his brother Harun was appointed as a helper alongside him.

chapters.heading: Before Pharaoh, Alongside Musa
chapters.narrative: Harun accompanied Musa to Pharaoh's court, both declaring themselves messengers of the Lord of the worlds and demanding the release of the Children of Israel. The fuller account of that confrontation, the staff and the white hand as signs, the contest with the magicians, the plagues, and the Exodus is told in Musa's own tale.

references.label: Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:10-51
references.gist: Musa and Harun together confront Pharaoh as messengers of the Lord of the worlds.

chapters.heading: The Golden Calf: Harun's Trial
chapters.narrative: While Musa was on Mount Sinai, the Israelites turned to worshipping a calf. Harun tried to stop them, warning that they were only being tested by it, and that their Lord was the Most Merciful, so they should follow him and obey his order. They refused, saying they would not stop until Musa returned. Harun feared that if he acted forcefully, he would fracture the community, and that Musa would then accuse him of causing division rather than obeying his instruction to keep things right. When Musa returned and saw the calf being worshipped, he was overcome with anger, threw down the Tablets, and seized his brother by the head and beard. Harun pleaded with him not to seize him by his beard or head, explaining he had feared Musa would say he had caused division among the Children of Israel and not observed his word. Musa then prayed for forgiveness for both himself and his brother.

references.label: Surah Al-A'raf 7:150
references.gist: Musa's anger on finding the calf worshipped; he seizes Harun and Harun defends himself.

references.label: Surah Ta-Ha 20:90-94
references.gist: Harun's warning to the people before Musa's return, and his explanation to Musa of why he did not act more forcefully.

name: Talut and Jalut
summary: Bani Isra'il asked their prophet for a king to lead them in battle, and Allah chose Talut (Saul), though the people objected that he was not wealthy. Talut led them out, tested them at a river, and marched the remainder against Jalut (Goliath) and his army. The young Dawud (David) killed Jalut, and Allah afterward gave Dawud kingship and wisdom. The Quran gives no specific date for this event.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:246-251
references.gist: Describes the Israelites asking for a king, Talut's appointment, the river test, and Dawud's killing of Jalut.

name: Dawud (AS)
lineage: A descendant of Ishaq (AS), many generations later.
summary: Given the Zabur (Psalms) and remembered as a prophet-king known for his justice, his beautiful voice in glorifying Allah, and skill in ironwork. Surah Sad recounts how, tested by a dispute brought before him, he realized his own hasty judgment, sought Allah's forgiveness, and repented.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:17-26
references.gist: Covers Dawud's strength in worship, the mountains and birds glorifying with him, and the parable of the two disputants.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:163
references.gist: Names Dawud among the prophets given revelation, and states he was given the Zabur.

tale.intro: Dawud's story in the Quran moves from a young soldier in the ranks of an army to a king given revelation, wisdom, and mastery over creation.

chapters.heading: The Young Soldier Who Slew Jalut
chapters.narrative: When the Children of Israel asked their prophet to appoint a king to lead them in battle, Talut was chosen, though some objected that he lacked wealth or lineage; the prophet told them Allah had chosen him and increased him in knowledge and stature, and that the Ark would be restored to them as a sign, carried by angels. Talut tested his army at a river, commanding that whoever drank from it was not with him except one who took only a handful; most of the army drank and turned back, leaving only a small band to cross with him. Facing the far larger army of Jalut, the faithful among them said that many a small company has overcome a large company by Allah's permission. In the battle that followed, they defeated their enemy by Allah's permission, and Dawud killed Jalut. Allah then gave Dawud kingship and wisdom, and taught him what He willed.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:246-251
references.gist: Talut is chosen king, the river test thins his army, and in the battle against Jalut's forces, Dawud kills Jalut.

chapters.heading: Kingship and the Zabur
chapters.narrative: The Quran lists Dawud among the prophets to whom Allah sent revelation, alongside Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, the tribes, Isa, Ayyub, Yunus, Harun, and Sulaiman, and states plainly that Dawud was given the Zabur.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:163
references.gist: Dawud is named among the prophets given revelation, and is specifically given the Zabur.

references.label: Surah Al-Isra 17:55
references.gist: Allah favored some prophets above others, and to Dawud He gave the Zabur.

chapters.heading: Mountains, Birds, and Iron Made Soft
chapters.narrative: Allah made the mountains and the birds glorify Him together with Dawud, and made iron soft and pliable in his hands, commanding him to make coats of mail and to measure their links well, so that he might have strength and be grateful. Dawud was given wisdom and sound judgment alongside this favor.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:79-80
references.gist: The mountains and birds glorify Allah with Dawud; he is taught the making of armor.

references.label: Surah Saba 34:10-11
references.gist: Mountains and birds glorify with him; iron is made soft in his hands to fashion well-measured coats of mail.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:17-20
references.gist: Dawud is praised for his strength in worship, and given wisdom and sound judgment.

chapters.heading: The Two Disputants
chapters.narrative: Two men climbed over the wall into Dawud's private chamber, startling him. They said they were disputants, one of whom had wronged the other, and asked him to judge between them with truth. One explained that his brother had ninety-nine ewes while he had only one, and that his brother wanted him to hand it over too, overpowering him in the argument. Dawud ruled that the man had wronged him in demanding his one ewe in addition to his own many, remarking that many partners wrong one another except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and these are few. Then Dawud realized Allah had tested him through the episode; he fell down in prostration and turned to his Lord in repentance, and was forgiven.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:21-25
references.gist: Two disputants bring Dawud the case of the ewes; he rules, then realizes it was a test and repents.

chapters.heading: The Fast of Dawud
chapters.narrative: Dawud's devotion became proverbial in later Islamic memory: the Prophet Muhammad described the fasting of Dawud, who used to fast on alternate days, as the most beloved voluntary fasting to Allah, a practice still known today as the fast of Dawud.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3420
references.gist: The Prophet states that the most beloved fasting to Allah was the fasting of Dawud, who fasted every other day.

name: Sulaiman (AS)
lineage: A direct son of Dawud (AS).
summary: The son of Dawud (AS), who inherited his father's prophethood and was given a vast kingdom, understanding of the speech of animals, and command over the jinn and the wind. His encounter with the Queen of Sheba, Bilqis, ends with her submitting to Allah alongside him.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:15-44
references.gist: Covers Sulaiman's inheritance from Dawud, the ants, the hoopoe's report, and the Queen of Sheba's submission.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:30-40
references.gist: Covers Sulaiman's prayer for an unmatched kingdom, the horses episode, and the wind and jinn subjected to him.

tale.intro: Sulaiman inherited his father Dawud's prophethood and kingship, and the Quran describes a rule unlike any other, over wind, jinn, and the speech of animals, and a famous encounter with a foreign queen who submitted to Allah.

chapters.heading: Inheriting Dawud
chapters.narrative: Sulaiman succeeded his father Dawud, telling the people they had been taught the language of birds, and had been given from all things, calling this an evident bounty.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:16
references.gist: Sulaiman inherits from Dawud and declares he has been taught the speech of birds and given from all things.

chapters.heading: A Prayer for an Unmatched Kingdom
chapters.narrative: Sulaiman prayed for forgiveness and for a kingdom that would not belong to anyone after him, since Allah was the Bestower.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:35
references.gist: Sulaiman asks Allah for forgiveness and for a kingdom unmatched by anyone who comes after him.

chapters.heading: Wind and Jinn at His Command
chapters.narrative: Allah subjected to Sulaiman a powerful wind that ran at his command toward the land He had blessed, its morning course equal to a month's journey and its evening course equal to another. He was also given a spring of molten copper, and jinn who worked before him by his Lord's permission, building what he willed, from places of worship to great basins and fixed cooking pots. Among them were divers who worked the sea retrieving pearls, and others restrained in chains, all subjected to his service.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:81-82
references.gist: The raging wind and diving jinn are subjected to Sulaiman by Allah's permission.

references.label: Surah Saba 34:12-13
references.gist: Wind, a spring of molten copper, and jinn laborers are placed at Sulaiman's command.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:36-38
references.gist: The wind flows gently at Sulaiman's order; jinn, including builders and divers, are subjected to him.

chapters.heading: The Valley of the Ants
chapters.narrative: Marching with his hosts of jinn, men, and birds, Sulaiman passed by a valley of ants, where one ant called out to the others to enter their dwellings so that Sulaiman and his soldiers would not crush them without perceiving it. Sulaiman smiled, amused at her words, and prayed to be grateful for Allah's favor upon him and his parents, to do righteous deeds pleasing to Him, and to be admitted by His mercy among His righteous servants.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:16-19
references.gist: An ant warns her colony of Sulaiman's approaching army; Sulaiman smiles and prays in gratitude.

chapters.heading: The Hoopoe's Report
chapters.narrative: Reviewing his birds, Sulaiman noticed the hoopoe was missing and threatened it with severe punishment unless it brought a clear excuse. The hoopoe arrived with news: it had come from Sheba with certain tidings, having found a woman ruling the people, given all she needed, and possessing a great throne. It reported that she and her people prostrated to the sun instead of Allah, led astray by Satan from the right path, so that they were not guided to worship the One who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and earth.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:20-26
references.gist: The hoopoe reports on the sun-worshipping Queen of Sheba and her people.

chapters.heading: The Letter and the Council
chapters.narrative: Sulaiman sent the hoopoe back with a letter, instructing it to deliver it and observe the response. Sealed in the name of Allah, the letter called on the queen and her people not to exalt themselves against him and to come to him in submission. She gathered her chiefs to consult them, noting that kings, when they enter a city by force, corrupt it and humiliate its honored people. Her advisors offered military strength but left the decision to her; she chose instead to send a gift, saying she would see what response her messengers brought back.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:27-35
references.gist: Sulaiman's letter is delivered; the queen consults her council and decides to send a gift instead of going to war.

chapters.heading: Bringing Her Throne
chapters.narrative: Before her delegation arrived, Sulaiman asked his assembly who could bring him her throne before she and her people came to him in submission. An ifrit among the jinn offered to bring it before Sulaiman could rise from his seat. But one who had knowledge of the Scripture said he would bring it in the blink of an eye, and he did. Seeing it set before him, Sulaiman recognized it as a test of his gratitude, saying it was by his Lord's favor, to see whether he would be grateful or ungrateful.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:38-40
references.gist: Sulaiman has the queen's throne brought to him instantly by one with knowledge of the Scripture, as a test of his gratitude.

chapters.heading: The Glass Floor and Her Submission
chapters.narrative: When Bilqis arrived, she was invited to enter the palace. Seeing its floor, she thought it a pool of water and bared her legs to wade through, but Sulaiman told her it was a smooth surface paved with glass. Recognizing the extent of what she had witnessed, she declared that she had wronged herself, and submitted with Sulaiman to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:44
references.gist: Bilqis mistakes the glass floor for water and, upon realizing her error, submits to Allah alongside Sulaiman.

chapters.heading: The Horses and Remembrance
chapters.narrative: One evening, fine, swift horses were displayed before Sulaiman, and he said he had come to love this wealth out of remembrance of his Lord, until they passed out of sight. He then commanded them brought back and began passing his hand over their legs and necks. Translators and commentators differ on exactly what this describes: some read it as Sulaiman affectionately caressing horses that had briefly absorbed his attention, others as an act of slaughtering some of them out of devotion after they distracted him from remembrance of Allah. The Arabic wording is genuinely ambiguous, so this account is presented here without resolving that dispute beyond what the text itself states.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:31-33
references.gist: Fine horses are displayed before Sulaiman; he expresses love for them out of remembrance of Allah, then handles them, the exact act is textually ambiguous.

chapters.heading: A Death Discovered by a Worm
chapters.narrative: When death was decreed for Sulaiman, nothing revealed it to the jinn except a worm of the earth that ate away at his staff, on which his body remained propped upright. When the staff finally gave way and he fell, it became clear to the jinn that, had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in humiliating labor, for they had continued working under him as though he still lived and watched over them.

references.label: Surah Saba 34:14
references.gist: Sulaiman's death goes unnoticed by the jinn until a worm eats through his staff and his body falls.

name: Ilyas (AS)
lineage: Islamic tradition places him among the descendants of Harun (AS), many generations later; this is not stated explicitly in the Quran.
summary: Sent to a people who worshipped the idol Ba'l instead of Allah, Ilyas called them back to pure monotheism. The Quran records that his rejecting people were seized for punishment, while Allah preserved his good name among later generations.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:123-132
references.gist: Covers Ilyas's call to his people away from worshipping Ba'l, their rejection, and the good name left for him among later generations.

references.label: Surah Al-An'am 6:85
references.gist: Names Ilyas among the righteous prophets guided by Allah.

tale.intro: The Quran preserves only a brief record of Ilyas (AS): his call to his people and his place among the righteous messengers.

chapters.heading: A Messenger Against the Worship of Ba'l
chapters.narrative: Ilyas was one of the messengers. He asked his people whether they would not fear Allah: would they call upon Ba'l and leave the best of creators, Allah, their Lord and the Lord of their first forefathers? They denied him, so all of them will be brought for punishment except Allah's chosen servants. Allah left for him a good name among later generations, peace upon Ilyas, as reward for the doers of good, for he was among Allah's believing servants.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:123-132
references.gist: Ilyas was among the messengers; he called his people away from worshipping Ba'l and toward Allah; they denied him except Allah's chosen servants; peace was left upon him among later generations, as reward for the doers of good, for he was among the believing servants.

name: Al-Yasa (AS)
lineage: Classical commentators identify him as the prophetic successor to Ilyas (AS); no blood relation between them is stated.
summary: Named in the Quran alongside other righteous prophets and honored as one preferred above the worlds. Classical commentators identify him as the prophetic successor to Ilyas (AS), continuing his mission of calling the Children of Israel back to monotheism.

references.label: Surah Al-An'am 6:86
references.gist: Names Al-Yasa among the prophets favored over other people of their time.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:48
references.gist: Names Al-Yasa alongside Isma'il and Dhul-Kifl as among the excellent.

tale.intro: Al-Yasa (AS) is named in the Quran only twice, each time as part of a list of the righteous; no narrative episode is attached to him.

chapters.heading: Named Among the Righteous
chapters.narrative: Al-Yasa is mentioned by name in two places in the Quran, both times as part of a list of prophets whom Allah guided and favored above other people, and elsewhere as one of the excellent ones among Allah's servants. No further detail, event, or teaching is recorded about him in the Quran, and no verified narrative hadith fills this in either; his place in the record is honorable but brief.

references.label: Surah Al-An'am 6:86
references.gist: Ishmael, Elisha (Al-Yasa), Jonah, and Lot, each favored over other people of their time.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:48
references.gist: Remember Our servants Ismail, Al-Yasa, and Dhul-Kifl, each of them among the excellent.

placementNote.text: Al-Yasa, Dhul-Kifl, and Yunus share this row because no Quran verse or hadith fixes their order relative to one another; grouping them together avoids implying a ranking the text doesn't state.

name: Dhul-Kifl (AS)
summary: Named in the Quran twice alongside other prophets and praised for his patience and righteousness. His precise historical identity is not agreed upon: most scholars count him among the prophets, though some hold he was a righteous, steadfast man rather than a prophet in his own right.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:85-86
references.gist: Names Dhul-Kifl alongside Isma'il and Idris as among the patient, admitted into Allah's mercy.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:48
references.gist: Names Dhul-Kifl alongside Isma'il and Al-Yasa as among the excellent.

tale.intro: Dhul-Kifl (AS) is named twice in the Quran and described as patient and righteous, but with no narrative episode attached, and even his prophethood has been debated among scholars.

chapters.heading: Patient, Righteous, and Excellent
chapters.narrative: Dhul-Kifl is named alongside Ismail and Idris as one of the patient, admitted into Allah's mercy among the righteous, and separately alongside Ismail and Al-Yasa as one of the excellent servants of Allah. The Quran gives no event, speech, or people connected to him beyond these descriptions. Because of this scant textual basis, some scholars have held he was a righteous, patient man rather than a prophet, while others count him among the prophets on the strength of his being named alongside them; the Quran itself does not settle the question.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:85-86
references.gist: Ismail, Idris, and Dhul-Kifl, all among the patient, admitted into Allah's mercy, among the righteous.

references.label: Surah Sad 38:48
references.gist: Remember Our servants Ismail, Al-Yasa, and Dhul-Kifl, each of them among the excellent.

placementNote.text: Al-Yasa, Dhul-Kifl, and Yunus share this row because no Quran verse or hadith fixes their order relative to one another; grouping them together avoids implying a ranking the text doesn't state.

name: Yunus (AS)
summary: Known as Dhun-Nun, 'the one of the fish.' He left his mission in frustration without Allah's permission and was swallowed by a great fish after being cast into the sea; from within it he cried out in repentance, and Allah delivered him.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:139-148
references.gist: Covers Yunus fleeing in anger, being swallowed by the fish, and his people believing in time to be spared.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:87-88
references.gist: Covers Yunus's prayer in the darkness of the fish's belly and Allah answering him.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3416
references.gist: The Prophet says no one should claim to be better than Yunus ibn Matta.

tale.intro: Yunus (AS) is the one prophet in the Quran whose people's punishment was lifted after they believed, but his own story begins with him leaving them before that happened.

chapters.heading: Sent to a People, and Leaving in Anger
chapters.narrative: Yunus was sent as a messenger to his people, though the Quran itself never names the city or nation he was sent to. Frustrated with his people, Yunus left them and went off in anger before his mission had run its course, assuming that Allah would not take him to task for it.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:139-140
references.gist: Yunus was among the messengers sent by Us; he ran away to the laden ship.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:87
references.gist: The man of the fish went off in anger, thinking We would not decree anything upon him.

chapters.heading: The Ship and the Lots
chapters.narrative: Yunus boarded a laden ship. When the ship was in danger, the crew cast lots to decide who would be thrown overboard, and the lot fell against Yunus.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:140-141
references.gist: He ran away to the laden ship, then shared in the casting of lots and was of the losers.

chapters.heading: Swallowed in Darkness
chapters.narrative: A great fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy in that moment. In the darkness, of the sea, the night, and the fish's belly together, he cried out: there is no deity except Allah, exalted is He, and he had been among the wrongdoers.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:142
references.gist: Then the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:87
references.gist: He called out within the darknesses: 'La ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu minaz-zalimin.'

chapters.heading: Cast onto the Shore, and the Plant
chapters.narrative: Had he not been among those who glorify Allah, he would have remained inside the fish until the Day of Resurrection. Allah answered him and saved him from distress, and this is how He saves the believers. He was cast onto a barren shore, unwell, and Allah caused a plant to grow over him for shade.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:143-144
references.gist: Had he not been of those who exalt Allah, he would have remained in its belly until the Day of Resurrection.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:88
references.gist: So We answered him and saved him from the distress; thus do We save the believers.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:145-146
references.gist: We cast him onto the open shore while he was ill, and We caused a plant of gourd to grow over him.

chapters.heading: Return, and a People Who Believed
chapters.narrative: Yunus was sent again to his people, a great multitude of a hundred thousand or more, and this time they believed. Because of that belief, Allah lifted the punishment of disgrace from them and let them live out their lives in comfort. The Quran names them explicitly as 'the people of Yunus', held up as the one community whose faith came in time to benefit them, after every other punished nation had refused to believe until it was too late.

references.label: Surah As-Saffat 37:147-148
references.gist: We sent him to a hundred thousand or more, and they believed, so We gave them enjoyment for a time.

references.label: Surah Yunus 10:98
references.gist: Has there not been a city that believed so its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace.

placementNote.text: Al-Yasa, Dhul-Kifl, and Yunus share this row because no Quran verse or hadith fixes their order relative to one another; grouping them together avoids implying a ranking the text doesn't state.

name: Zakariya (AS)
summary: The guardian of Maryam, who witnessed Allah providing for her miraculously and was inspired to pray for a child of his own despite his old age and his wife's barrenness. Allah answered him with the glad tidings of a son, Yahya, given a sign that he would not speak to people for three days and nights.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:2-15
references.gist: Covers Zakariya's private prayer for an heir, the glad tidings of Yahya, and his sign of three days' silence.

references.label: Surah Aal-Imran 3:37-41
references.gist: Covers Zakariya's guardianship of Maryam, his prayer in the sanctuary, and the announcement of Yahya's birth.

tale.intro: Zakariya (AS) prayed for a son in his old age, alongside a life already spent as the guardian of Maryam.

chapters.heading: Guardian of Maryam
chapters.narrative: Maryam's Lord accepted her graciously and made her grow in goodness, and He placed her in the care of Zakariya. Whenever Zakariya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found provision with her. He asked her where it came from, and she answered that it was from Allah, who provides for whom He wills without account.

references.label: Surah Ali 'Imran 3:37
references.gist: Allah made Zakariya Maryam's guardian; he found provision with her in the sanctuary and she told him it was from Allah.

chapters.heading: A Private Prayer for an Heir
chapters.narrative: It was seeing Allah's provision come to Maryam without any apparent source that moved Zakariya to pray to his Lord there, asking for a good, righteous offspring of his own. He called upon his Lord quietly, saying that his bones had weakened and his head had turned gray with age, and that he had never been disappointed in his prayer before. He feared what his kinsmen would do after him, and his wife was barren, so he asked Allah to grant him from Himself an heir who would inherit from him and from the family of Yaqub, and asked that Allah make him pleasing.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:2-6
references.gist: Zakariya's quiet prayer: his bones have weakened, his hair has grayed, he fears his kinsmen after him, his wife is barren, grant me an heir.

references.label: Surah Ali 'Imran 3:38
references.gist: There, Zakariya called upon his Lord, saying: My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring.

chapters.heading: Glad Tidings, a Sign, and Silence
chapters.narrative: Allah answered him with good tidings of a boy named Yahya, for whom no equal had been made before. Zakariya, astonished, asked how he could have a son when his wife was barren and he himself had reached extreme old age. He was told this was so, easy for his Lord, who had created him before out of nothing. Zakariya then asked for a sign, and was told his sign would be that he would not speak to people for three days though he was sound of body, able only to communicate by gesture. He went out to his people from the sanctuary and signaled to them to glorify Allah morning and evening.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:7-11
references.gist: Glad tidings of Yahya; Zakariya's astonishment; his sign of three days' silence though sound in body; he gestured to his people to glorify Allah.

references.label: Surah Ali 'Imran 3:39-41
references.gist: The angels called to him while he stood praying in the sanctuary, giving glad tidings of Yahya; he asked for a sign and was given three days of speaking to people only by gesture.

name: Yahya (AS)
lineage: A direct son of Zakariya (AS).
summary: The son of Zakariya (AS), given wisdom by Allah while still a child and described as pure, dutiful to his parents, and never insolent or rebellious. He is honored in the Quran with the greeting of peace upon the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:12-15
references.gist: Covers Yahya being given wisdom as a child, his devotion to his parents, and the peace decreed upon him.

references.label: Surah Aal-Imran 3:38-39
references.gist: Covers the angels announcing Yahya's birth to Zakariya while he stood praying in the sanctuary.

tale.intro: Yahya (AS) was the answer to Zakariya's private prayer, described in the Quran chiefly through his character.

chapters.heading: Wisdom, Purity, and Devotion to His Parents
chapters.narrative: Yahya was commanded, while still a child, to hold firmly to the Scripture, and Allah gave him wisdom while he was yet young, along with tenderness and purity from Him. He was mindful of Allah, and dutiful to his parents, and he was not insolent or disobedient.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:12-14
references.gist: Yahya was given wisdom, tenderness, and purity while a child; he was God-fearing and dutiful to his parents, neither a tyrant nor disobedient.

chapters.heading: Peace at Birth, Death, and Resurrection
chapters.narrative: Peace was decreed upon him on the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive again.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:15
references.gist: And peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.

name: Isa (AS)
lineage: A descendant of Ishaq (AS), many generations later, through the lineage of Bani Isra'il.
summary: Born miraculously to Maryam without a father. Allah gave him the Injeel and, by Allah's permission, the ability to heal the sick and raise the dead. Islamic teaching holds that he was raised to Allah rather than killed, and that he will return before the Day of Judgment.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:16-35
references.gist: Covers the angel's announcement to Maryam, Isa's birth beneath the palm tree, and the infant speaking from the cradle.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:110-120
references.gist: Covers Isa's miracles by Allah's permission, the disciples and the table from heaven, and his denial of having told people to worship him.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3448
references.gist: The Prophet says Isa will descend as a just ruler, break the cross, kill the pig, and abolish the jizyah tax.

tale.intro: Isa (AS)'s birth, miracles, and the Quran's own account of his end are covered here; his second coming near the end of times is covered separately in the End Times entry, The Descent of Isa.

chapters.heading: The Angel's Announcement to Maryam
chapters.narrative: While Maryam had withdrawn from her family to a place to the east, Allah sent His angel to her in the form of a well-proportioned man. She was frightened and sought refuge from him, but he told her he was only a messenger from her Lord, sent to give her a pure boy. She asked how she could have a son when no man had touched her and she was not unchaste. He answered that it was so, easy for her Lord, who would make the boy a sign for mankind and a mercy, and that the matter was already decreed. In Surah Ali 'Imran, the angels likewise give her the news that Allah gives her glad tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, honored in this world and the next, who will speak to people in the cradle and in maturity, among the righteous.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:16-21
references.gist: The angel appears to Maryam, announces a pure son, and tells her it is easy for her Lord and already decreed.

references.label: Surah Ali 'Imran 3:45-47
references.gist: The angels announce a word from Allah, named the Messiah Isa son of Maryam, who will speak to people in the cradle and in maturity.

chapters.heading: Birth Beneath the Palm Tree
chapters.narrative: Maryam conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place. Labor pains drove her to the trunk of a palm tree, and she cried out that she wished she had died before this and been forgotten entirely. A voice called to her from below, telling her not to grieve: her Lord had placed a stream beneath her, and she should shake the trunk of the palm tree so that ripe, fresh dates would fall to her. She was told to eat, drink, and be comforted, and if she saw anyone, to say she had vowed a fast of silence to the Most Merciful and would not speak to any human that day.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:22-26
references.gist: Maryam gives birth by the palm tree; a stream and falling dates are provided for her; she is told to keep a vow of silence.

chapters.heading: The Infant Speaks from the Cradle
chapters.narrative: She brought the child to her people, carrying him. They accused her of a strange thing, that her father had not been a man of evil nor her mother unchaste. She pointed to the infant. They asked how they could speak to one who was a child in the cradle. The baby spoke: he was the servant of Allah, given the Scripture and made a prophet, made blessed wherever he was, enjoined with prayer and zakah as long as he remained alive, and dutifulness to his mother, not made a wretched tyrant. Peace was on him the day he was born, the day he would die, and the day he would be raised alive.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:27-33
references.gist: Maryam's people accuse her; the infant Isa speaks from the cradle, declaring himself a servant of Allah given the Scripture and prophethood.

chapters.heading: A Messenger's Miracles, by Allah's Leave
chapters.narrative: As a messenger to the Children of Israel, Isa declared he had come with a sign from their Lord: that he would fashion for them, out of clay, the shape of a bird, then breathe into it, and it would become a real bird by Allah's permission; that he would heal the blind and the leper, and raise the dead, all by Allah's permission; and that he could tell them what they ate and what they stored in their houses. Allah later reminds Isa of this favor directly: that He strengthened him with the Holy Spirit so that he spoke to people in infancy and in maturity, and that by Allah's permission he shaped clay into the form of a bird and it became a bird, healed the blind and the leper, and raised the dead, always by Allah's permission, never his own power.

references.label: Surah Ali 'Imran 3:49
references.gist: Isa's own proclamation of the sign he brings: shaping a bird from clay and giving it life, healing the blind and leper, raising the dead, all by Allah's leave.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:110
references.gist: Allah reminds Isa of His favor: strengthening him with the Holy Spirit, and enabling the clay-bird miracle, the healings, and raising the dead, all by Allah's permission.

chapters.heading: The Disciples and the Table from Heaven
chapters.narrative: Allah inspired the disciples to believe in Him and His messenger, and they declared their belief and submission. The disciples asked Isa whether his Lord could send down to them a table spread with food from heaven. Isa told them to fear Allah if they were believers. They said they wished to eat from it, to have their hearts reassured, to know he had told them the truth, and to be witnesses to it. Isa prayed for it to be sent down as a festival for them and a sign from Allah. Allah answered that He would send it down, but warned that whoever disbelieved after that among them would be punished with a punishment unlike any given to others in the worlds.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:111-115
references.gist: The disciples ask for a table spread from heaven; Isa prays for it; Allah agrees to send it, with a severe warning against disbelief afterward.

chapters.heading: Neither Killed Nor Crucified
chapters.narrative: Regarding the claim of killing the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of Allah, the Quran states plainly that they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them. Those who differed about it are described as being in doubt, having no real knowledge, only following assumption; they did not kill him with certainty. Rather, Allah raised him to Himself, and Allah is exalted in might and wise.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:157-158
references.gist: They did not kill him or crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them; Allah raised him to Himself.

chapters.heading: A Sign, Not a Deity
chapters.narrative: The Quran warns against exceeding bounds in religion regarding Isa: the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, was only a messenger of Allah, His word which He conveyed to Maryam, and a spirit from Him, so people should believe in Allah and His messengers and not speak of a Trinity, since Allah is only one God, far above having a son. Elsewhere, Allah addresses Isa directly on the Day of Judgment, asking whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods besides Allah. Isa's reply is a denial: it was not for him to say what he had no right to say; he said only what he was commanded, to worship Allah, his Lord and their Lord.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:171
references.gist: The Messiah Isa was only a messenger of Allah and His word conveyed to Maryam and a spirit from Him; Allah is one, far above having a son.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:116-117
references.gist: Allah asks Isa if he told people to worship him and his mother; Isa denies it, saying he told them only to worship Allah.

placementNote.text: Isa's line back to Ishaq is recorded, but the Quran and hadith don't preserve every generation between them, which is why the connecting line on this tree runs so far down from Ishaq's row. His own row reflects his place as the last prophet sent to the Children of Israel before Muhammad (SAW).

name: Muhammad (SAW)
lineage: A descendant of Isma'il (AS), many generations later.
summary: The final messenger of Allah and a mercy to all of creation. He received the Quran over twenty-three years and delivered the complete and final message of Islam, after which Allah sent no further prophet.

family.name: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid
family.note: First wife, married before prophethood, mother of all his children except Ibrahim. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari is devoted to this marriage and her standing; the Quran does not name her.

family.name: Sawdah bint Zam'ah
family.note: Married after Khadijah's death. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari names her directly, describing how in her old age she gave up her turn with the Prophet to Aisha. Scholars differ on whether Sawdah or Aisha married the Prophet first: by marriage contract Aisha's came first, but Sawdah's marriage was consummated first, which is why she is usually placed second in the sequence and Aisha third; this specific ordering is seerah convention, not a claim made by the hadith below.

family.name: Aisha bint Abi Bakr
family.note: Extensively documented in hadith literature as a primary narrator, including a hadith describing her age at marriage and at its consummation. See the note on Sawdah for the contract-versus-consummation ordering dispute between the two.

family.name: Hafsah bint Umar
family.note: Daughter of the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari names her, together with Aisha, as the two wives addressed in Quran 66:4.

family.name: Umm Salamah (Hind bint Abi Umayyah)
family.note: A hadith in Sunan an-Nasa'i narrates how, after her waiting period ended and Abu Bakr's proposal was declined, the Prophet proposed through Umar, and her son performed the marriage at her request.

family.name: Zaynab bint Jahsh
family.note: Her marriage is connected to Quran 33:37, the only case where a Quranic verse addresses the circumstances of one of the Prophet's marriages directly, though it does not use her name.

family.name: Juwayriyyah bint al-Harith
family.note: A hadith narrated by Ibn Abbas, in Imam al-Bukhari's Al-Adab Al-Mufrad, records that the Prophet changed her name from Barrah to Juwayriyyah after marrying her.

family.name: Safiyyah bint Huyayy
family.note: A hadith in Sahih Muslim describes her wedding feast after the Battle of Khaybar. Her marriage and Umm Habibah's are order-disputed: Umm Habibah's marriage contract came earlier by proxy, but Safiyyah's marriage was consummated first, which is why she is usually placed ninth and Umm Habibah tenth; this ordering itself is seerah convention, not a specific hadith's claim.

family.name: Umm Habibah (Ramlah bint Abi Sufyan)
family.note: A hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud describes how the Negus of Abyssinia married her to the Prophet by proxy after her first husband's death, with a dower on the Prophet's behalf. See the note on Safiyyah for the ordering dispute between them.

family.name: Maymunah bint al-Harith
family.note: The last of the eleven Ummahat al-Mu'minin married. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari names her directly, in the context of a dispute among later scholars over whether the marriage took place during or after the state of ihram.

family.name: Fatimah
family.note: Youngest daughter, from Khadijah, and the most prominent of his children; the only child to outlive him by a significant span.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3714
references.gist: The Prophet says Fatimah is a part of him, and whoever angers her angers him.

family.name: Al-Qasim
family.note: From Khadijah; died in infancy. The Prophet's kunya, Abu al-Qasim, derives from him.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3537
references.gist: After a man calls out to him as Abu al-Qasim in the marketplace, the Prophet says people may name themselves after him but not take his kunya.

family.name: Ibrahim
family.note: Died in infancy; the only child not born to Khadijah. His mother is not named in Sahih al-Bukhari or Sahih Muslim.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1043
references.gist: Narrates that a solar eclipse occurred on the day the Prophet's son Ibrahim died, and the Prophet corrected people who linked the two, saying the sun and moon do not eclipse for anyone's death.

references.label: Surah Al-Ahzab 33:40
references.gist: States Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets, after whom no further prophet is sent.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:107
references.gist: States the Prophet was sent as a mercy to all the worlds.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3535
references.gist: The Prophet compares himself and the prophets before him to a house built except for one missing brick, saying he is that brick and the last of the Prophets.

tale.intro: Muhammad's (SAW) life is also told chronologically, event by event, across the Timeline tab; this tale draws that same cited material together into one connected account, from his birth to his death.

chapters.heading: Born an Orphan
chapters.narrative: Muhammad was born in Makkah. His father, Abdullah, had already died before he was born. Allah later reminded him of this directly in revelation: had He not found him an orphan and sheltered him, found him unaware and guided him, found him in need and made him self-sufficient. His mother, Aminah, died when he was six, and he was then raised by his grandfather Abdul-Muttalib and, after his grandfather's death two years later, by his uncle Abu Talib. That part of his upbringing, his mother's death and his grandfather's and uncle's guardianship, is well established in early seerah works, but no specific Quran verse or authenticated hadith with a confirmed citation was found narrating it, so it is included here without a reference, in the same way as the Boycott of Banu Hashim and the Year of Sorrow later in this tale.

references.label: Surah Ad-Duha 93:6-8
references.gist: Reminds the Prophet that Allah found him an orphan and sheltered him, found him unaware and guided him, found him in need and made him self-sufficient.

chapters.heading: Marriage to Khadijah
chapters.narrative: Before his prophethood, Muhammad married Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a respected Makkan businesswoman. She was his first wife and the mother of all his children except Ibrahim, and remained his only wife until her death. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari is devoted to this marriage and to her standing with him; the Quran itself does not name her.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3821
references.gist: Narrates the marriage of Khadijah to the Prophet and her standing as his first wife.

chapters.heading: The First Revelation
chapters.narrative: While in seclusion in the Cave of Hira outside Makkah, at forty years old, the angel Jibril came to him and commanded him to read, revealing the opening verses of Surah Al-Alaq, the first revelation. Terrified, he returned home to Khadijah asking to be covered, and she reassured him, later taking him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, who recognized the description as matching the revelation given to earlier prophets. This episode is narrated at length in the very first hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari's Book of Revelation. A period of pause in revelation followed; a hadith narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah describes him then seeing the same angel again, seated between heaven and earth, after which he returned home shaken and asked to be wrapped, and the opening verses of Surah Al-Muddaththir, 'O you wrapped in garments, arise and warn,' were revealed, making it the second revelation.

references.label: Surah Al-Alaq 96:1-5
references.gist: The first revealed verses, commanding the Prophet to read, in the name of his Lord who created.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3
references.gist: Aisha's narration of the first revelation at the Cave of Hira, and Khadijah taking him to Waraqah ibn Nawfal.

references.label: Surah Al-Muddaththir 74:1-7
references.gist: The second revelation, commanding him to arise and warn.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4
references.gist: Jabir ibn Abdullah's narration of the pause in revelation and the second appearance of the angel.

chapters.heading: Migration to Abyssinia
chapters.narrative: As persecution of the early Muslims in Makkah intensified, he directed a group of his followers to migrate to Abyssinia, ruled by a Christian king, the Negus, known for his justice. When a Quraysh delegation pursued them to demand their return, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib spoke on the Muslims' behalf before the Negus, reciting the opening of Surah Maryam. A hadith in Musnad Ahmad records that the Negus and his bishops wept until their scriptures were wet with tears, and refused to hand the Muslims back over.

references.label: Musnad Ahmad 1740
references.gist: Narrates Ja'far's recitation before the Negus and the Negus's refusal to return the Muslim migrants to the Quraysh delegation.

chapters.heading: The Splitting of the Moon
chapters.narrative: At some point in the Makkan period, whose exact year these narrations do not fix, the Quran records that the moon split, opening Surah Al-Qamar by stating the Hour has drawn near and the moon has split. Several companions independently narrate having witnessed this, including Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud, the last of whom says the Prophet told those present, 'Bear witness.'

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:1-2
references.gist: States the Hour has drawn near and the moon has split.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3636
references.gist: A companion's narration of witnessing the moon split into two visible parts.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2802a
references.gist: Anas ibn Malik narrates that the people of Makkah demanded a sign from the Prophet, and he showed them the moon split in two.

chapters.heading: The Journey to Ta'if
chapters.narrative: Facing intensifying persecution in Makkah, he traveled to the nearby town of Ta'if seeking support and protection, but its leaders rejected him and set their slaves and children to pelt him with stones until he bled, forcing him to retreat. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha later asked him whether he had faced a harder day than the Battle of Uhud, and he described this day as the hardest, recounting that the angel of the mountains offered to crush the town between two mountains, and he refused, hoping Allah would bring believers from among their descendants instead.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3231
references.gist: The Prophet describes the rejection and stoning at Ta'if as harder than Uhud, and declines the angel's offer to destroy the town.

chapters.heading: Isra and Mi'raj
chapters.narrative: In a single night, he was taken from Makkah to the Farthest Mosque in Jerusalem, then ascended through the heavens, meeting earlier prophets and reaching a station in the presence of Allah. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari narrates that prayer was made obligatory during this journey, originally fifty times a day, reduced to five after Musa repeatedly advised him to ask for a reduction, with Allah counting the five as equal in reward to fifty.

references.label: Surah Al-Isra 17:1
references.gist: States that Allah took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 349
references.gist: The Mi'raj narration in which the five daily prayers are fixed after being reduced from fifty.

chapters.heading: The Hijra to Madinah
chapters.narrative: Facing a Quraysh plot to kill him, he migrated from Makkah to Madinah with Abu Bakr, first hiding for three days in the Cave of Thawr while their pursuers searched nearby. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari narrates that when Abu Bakr feared they would be seen, he reassured him: 'What do you think of two, when Allah is their third?' The Quran itself references this episode directly, saying Allah helped him when the disbelievers drove him out, when the two of them were in the cave, and he told his companion not to grieve, for Allah was with them. This migration marks the start of the Islamic calendar.

references.label: Surah At-Tawbah 9:40
references.gist: Recounts Allah's help in the cave during the migration, and the Prophet's reassurance to his companion.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4663
references.gist: Narrates the moment in the Cave of Thawr, with the Prophet's words: 'What do you think of two, when Allah is their third?'

chapters.heading: The Change of the Qibla
chapters.narrative: After praying toward Jerusalem for about sixteen or seventeen months since the Hijra, he was commanded to turn instead toward the Kaaba in Makkah. A hadith narrated by Al-Bara ibn Azib describes the moment: the command arrived mid-prayer during Asr, the congregation immediately turned to face the Kaaba, and word reached another group still bowing in a separate mosque, who turned as well while still in that position. The Quran addresses the change at length, anticipating objections from those who would question it.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:142-150
references.gist: Addresses the change of the qibla from Jerusalem to the Kaaba, anticipating objections to it.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4486
references.gist: Narrates the moment the command to change the qibla reached the Muslims mid-prayer.

chapters.heading: Battle of Badr
chapters.narrative: Fought on 17 Ramadan, 2 AH, this was the first major battle between the Muslims of Madinah and the Quraysh of Makkah. A Muslim force of about 300 faced a Quraysh army roughly three times its size and won decisively. The Quran attributes the victory to Allah's help, including the sending of angels, and calls the day the day the criterion was revealed.

references.label: Surah Aal-Imran 3:123-125
references.gist: Recalls Allah's help at Badr despite the Muslims being weak, including the sending of angels.

references.label: Surah Al-Anfal 8:5-19
references.gist: Discusses the events and lessons of the Battle of Badr at length.

chapters.heading: Battle of Uhud
chapters.narrative: Fought near Mount Uhud outside Madinah, this battle came as the Quraysh returned to avenge their defeat at Badr. The Muslims held the advantage until a group of archers left their assigned position to gather spoils, allowing the Quraysh cavalry to attack from the rear. The Muslims suffered significant losses, and the Quran addresses the battle at length, including the lessons of the archers' disobedience.

references.label: Surah Aal-Imran 3:121-175
references.gist: Addresses the Battle of Uhud at length, including the archers' disobedience and its consequences.

chapters.heading: Battle of the Trench
chapters.narrative: A confederation of Quraysh, Ghatafan, and allied tribes, numbering around 10,000, besieged Madinah. The Muslims dug a defensive trench around the exposed side of the city, a tactic unfamiliar to the Arabs, which neutralized the confederate cavalry. After a siege of roughly a month, a severe windstorm scattered the confederate camp and the siege was lifted without a pitched battle. The Quran describes the intensity of this trial for the believers.

references.label: Surah Al-Ahzab 33:9-27
references.gist: Describes the siege of Madinah, the trench, and the intensity of the trial for the believers.

chapters.heading: The Judgment on Banu Qurayza
chapters.narrative: After the Trench, the Muslims besieged Banu Qurayza, a Jewish tribe in Madinah accused of breaking their treaty with the Muslims by aiding the confederate siege. Banu Qurayza agreed to accept the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, an ally they themselves had proposed, on the condition that he decide their fate. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari records that Sa'd ruled that their fighting men be killed and their women and children taken captive, and that the Prophet said this matched Allah's judgment. This is a historically and ethically weighty episode, reported here exactly as the hadith states it, without embellishment in either direction.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4121
references.gist: Narrates Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's judgment on Banu Qurayza and the Prophet's confirmation of it.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3043
references.gist: A parallel narration of the same judgment.

chapters.heading: Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
chapters.narrative: He set out with his companions to perform Umrah but was stopped by the Quraysh outside Makkah at Hudaybiyyah. A ten-year truce was negotiated: the Muslims would return that year without completing the Umrah but could return to perform it the following year. Many companions saw the terms as unfavorable, but Surah Al-Fath, revealed shortly after, calls the treaty a clear victory.

references.label: Surah Al-Fath 48:1-29
references.gist: Calls the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah a clear victory, revealed shortly after it was concluded.

chapters.heading: Battle of Khaybar
chapters.narrative: He led the Muslims against Khaybar, a cluster of Jewish fortresses north of Madinah, after the community there had been implicated in hostile alliances against the Muslims. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari records him announcing before the final fort fell that he would give the standard to a man through whom Allah would grant victory, which went to Ali.
