After the conquest, a Jewish woman presented him with a roasted sheep she had poisoned; he spat out the piece he had tasted, and a companion who had swallowed more, Bishr ibn al-Bara, later died from it.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3009
references.gist: Narrates the Prophet giving the standard to Ali before the final fort of Khaybar fell.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3169
references.gist: Narrates the poisoned sheep incident after the conquest of Khaybar.

chapters.heading: Battle of Mu'tah
chapters.narrative: He sent an army north to Mu'tah, in modern Jordan, against Byzantine-aligned forces, appointing Zayd ibn Harithah as commander, with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and then Abdullah ibn Rawahah to succeed him if he fell. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari narrates that he, still in Madinah, announced the battle's outcome as it happened far away, saying with tears in his eyes that Zayd took the flag and was martyred, then Ja'far took it and was martyred, then Ibn Rawahah took it and was martyred.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4262
references.gist: Narrates the Prophet announcing, from Madinah, the deaths of the three successive commanders at Mu'tah.

chapters.heading: Conquest of Makkah
chapters.narrative: After the Quraysh broke the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah by aiding an attack on his allies, he marched on Makkah with a large force, entering the city around 20 Ramadan, 8 AH, with almost no resistance. He declared a general amnesty for the Makkans, had the idols around the Kaaba destroyed, and the city's population largely accepted Islam in the following period. As he struck down the 360 idols surrounding the Kaaba, he recited, 'Truth has come and falsehood has vanished; falsehood is ever bound to vanish.'

references.label: Surah Al-Isra 17:81
references.gist: States that truth has come and falsehood has vanished, for falsehood is ever bound to vanish, the verse the Prophet recited while destroying the idols at the Kaaba.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4720
references.gist: Ibn Masud narrates the Prophet entering Makkah, finding 360 idols around the Kaaba, and striking them down while reciting that truth has come and falsehood has vanished.

chapters.heading: Battle of Hunayn
chapters.narrative: Shortly after the conquest of Makkah, the Muslim army, now swelled to about 12,000 including recent Makkan converts, marched against the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes in the Hunayn valley. An ambush in a narrow pass initially threw the Muslim front ranks into disarray, but he rallied his companions and the Muslims won a decisive victory. The Quran addresses the momentary overconfidence in numbers and the divine help that followed.

references.label: Surah At-Tawbah 9:25-26
references.gist: Addresses the overconfidence in numbers at Hunayn, followed by Allah's help and tranquility sent down.

chapters.heading: Expedition of Tabuk
chapters.narrative: He led roughly 30,000 Muslims north to Tabuk in response to reports of a Byzantine military buildup, in the largest and most difficult expedition of his life, undertaken in extreme heat during a period of drought. No battle was fought; the Byzantine force did not appear, and he secured treaties with several regional rulers before returning to Madinah. A large portion of Surah At-Tawbah addresses this expedition.

references.label: Surah At-Tawbah 9:38-129
references.gist: Addresses the expedition of Tabuk at length, including those who held back from it.

chapters.heading: The Farewell Pilgrimage
chapters.narrative: This was his only Hajj as a Muslim leader. During this pilgrimage he delivered the Farewell Sermon, addressing the sanctity of life and property, the rights of women, the abolition of usury and pre-Islamic blood feuds, and the equality of believers. A hadith narrates that Umar was later asked by a Jewish man which day Quran 5:3, 'today I have perfected your religion for you,' was revealed on, and Umar answered precisely: the evening of the Day of Arafah, a Friday, during this pilgrimage.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:3
references.gist: States that Allah has this day perfected the religion and completed His favor.

references.label: Musnad Ahmad 188
references.gist: Umar identifies the exact day 5:3 was revealed as the evening of Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

chapters.heading: The Death of the Prophet
chapters.narrative: Not long after the Farewell Pilgrimage, he fell into his final illness. Aisha narrates that he was leaning against her chest; he dipped his hand in water and wiped his face with it, saying, 'La ilaha illa Allah, indeed death has its agonies.' He then lifted his hand toward the sky, saying, 'with the highest companion,' until he died and his hand fell. He was sixty-three years old.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4449
references.gist: Aisha's firsthand narration of the Prophet's final moments: leaning against her chest, dipping his hand in water, saying death has its agonies, then repeating 'with the highest companion' until he died.

placementNote.text: Muhammad (SAW) is placed last because the Quran explicitly calls him the seal of the prophets, after whom no further prophet was sent.

references.label: Surah Al-Ahzab 33:40
references.gist: States Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets.

name: The Companions of the Elephant (Ashab al-Fil)
summary: Abraha, the Abyssinian governor of Yemen, marched on Makkah with an army that included elephants, intending to destroy the Kaaba. As they approached, Allah sent flocks of birds pelting them with stones of baked clay, striking them down and leaving them like husks of eaten grain, and the army never reached the House.

references.label: Surah Al-Fil 105:1-5
references.gist: Describes Allah foiling the Army of the Elephant, sending birds that pelted them with stones of baked clay and left them like eaten straw.

name: The First Revelation
summary: While in seclusion in the Cave of Hira outside Makkah, the angel Jibril came to the Prophet and commanded him to read, revealing the opening verses of Surah Al-Alaq, the first revelation. Terrified, he returned home to Khadijah asking to be covered, and she reassured him, later taking him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, who recognized the description as matching the revelation given to earlier prophets. This episode is narrated at length in the very first hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari's Book of Revelation. A period of pause in revelation followed; a hadith narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah describes the Prophet then seeing the same angel again, seated between heaven and earth, after which he returned home shaken and asked to be wrapped, and the opening verses of Surah Al-Muddaththir ('O you wrapped in garments, arise and warn') were revealed, making it the second revelation.

provenDates.label: The Prophet was 40 years old when this took place

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3851
references.gist: Ibn Abbas: the Prophet was inspired at the age of forty, then stayed in Mecca thirteen years and in Medina ten, until his death.

provenDates.label: Took place in the month of Ramadan

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:185
references.gist: States that the Quran was sent down in the month of Ramadan.

references.label: Surah Al-Alaq 96:1-5
references.gist: The first revealed verses, commanding the Prophet to read in the name of his Lord who created.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3
references.gist: Aisha's narration of the first revelation at the Cave of Hira and Khadijah taking the Prophet to Waraqah ibn Nawfal.

references.label: Surah Al-Muddaththir 74:1-7
references.gist: The second revelation, commanding the Prophet to arise and warn.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4
references.gist: Jabir ibn Abdullah's narration of the pause in revelation and the second appearance of the angel.

name: Migration to Abyssinia
summary: As persecution of the early Muslims in Makkah intensified, the Prophet directed a group of his followers to migrate to Abyssinia (modern Ethiopia), ruled by a Christian king, the Negus (An-Najashi), known for his justice. When a Quraysh delegation pursued them to demand their return, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib spoke on the Muslims' behalf before the Negus, reciting the opening of Surah Maryam; a hadith in Musnad Ahmad records that the Negus and his bishops wept until their scriptures were wet with tears, and refused to hand the Muslims back over.

references.label: Musnad Ahmad 1740
references.gist: Narrates Ja'far ibn Abi Talib reciting the opening of Surah Maryam before the Negus, who wept and refused to return the Muslim migrants to the Quraysh delegation.

name: The Splitting of the Moon
summary: The Quran opens Surah Al-Qamar by stating the Hour has drawn near and the moon has split, which classical commentators and multiple companions' hadith connect to a specific miracle witnessed in Makkah: the moon appearing to split into two visible parts. Several companions independently narrate having seen it, including Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud, the last of whom says the Prophet told them, 'Bear witness.' The exact year is not fixed by these narrations.

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:1-2
references.gist: States the Hour has drawn near and the moon has split.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3636
references.gist: Ibn Mas'ud's narration of witnessing the moon split into two visible parts, with the Prophet telling those present to bear witness.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2802a
references.gist: Anas ibn Malik narrates that the people of Makkah demanded a sign from the Prophet, and he showed them the moon split in two.

name: The Journey to Ta'if
summary: Facing intensifying persecution in Makkah, the Prophet traveled to the nearby town of Ta'if seeking support and protection, but its leaders rejected him and set their slaves and children to pelt him with stones until he bled, forcing him to retreat. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha later asked him whether he had faced a harder day than the Battle of Uhud, and he described this day as the hardest, recounting that the angel of the mountains offered to crush the town between two mountains, and he refused, hoping Allah would bring believers from among their descendants instead.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3231

summary: The Prophet used to deliver his sermons leaning against a palm trunk in the mosque. When a pulpit was built and he began using it instead, the trunk was heard crying, and he went to it and placed his hand on it until it settled.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3583

He was sixty-three years old. This hadith is one of the most detailed firsthand accounts of his death, narrated by the wife who was present.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3536
references.gist: Anas ibn Malik: Allah's Messenger died when he was sixty-three years old.

provenDates.label: 23 years of prophethood: 13 in Makkah, 10 in Madinah

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3851
references.gist: Ibn Abbas: the Prophet was inspired at forty, stayed in Mecca thirteen years, then in Medina ten years, then died.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1387
references.gist: Aisha, asked by Abu Bakr which day the Prophet died, answers: he died on Monday.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4449
references.gist: Aisha's firsthand narration of the Prophet's final moments: leaning against her chest, dipping his hand in water, saying death has its agonies, then repeating 'with the highest companion' until he died.

name: Barzakh, the Intermediate Realm
summary: The state between death and resurrection, named directly in the Quran as a barrier the dead cannot cross back through.

references.label: Surah Al-Mu'minun 23:100
references.gist: States that behind the dead is a barzakh (barrier) until the Day they are resurrected, so they cannot return to worldly life.

references.label: Surah Ghafir 40:46
references.gist: Describes Pharaoh's people exposed to the Fire morning and evening before the Hour, then to the severest punishment when the Hour is established; classical tafsir reads this as evidence of punishment in the grave, a lesser torment now followed by a greater one on Judgment Day.

name: The Trial and Punishment of the Grave
summary: What happens between death and the grave: at the moment of death itself, the believer's soul is drawn out gently, met by angels bearing Paradise's shrouds and fragrance, while the disbeliever's soul is wrenched out harshly. In the grave, two angels then question the deceased, and the grave itself becomes either comfort or punishment. The two angels, Munkar and Nakir, are covered in the Angels tab (search for their names to jump straight there).

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 4753
references.gist: The long hadith of a funeral: angels with Paradise's shrouds and fragrance draw the believer's soul out gently, against the disbeliever's soul being wrenched out harshly, followed by the three questions asked in the grave, who is your Lord, what is your religion, who is this man sent to you.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1361
references.gist: The Prophet passes two graves and says both occupants are being punished, one for not guarding against his own urine, the other for going about spreading slander.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 588a
references.gist: Teaches seeking refuge with Allah, at the end of every prayer's final tashahhud, from four trials: the torment of Hell, the torment of the grave, the trial of life and death, and the Dajjal.

name: Ad-Dukhan, the Smoke
summary: Surah Ad-Dukhan warns of a day when the sky produces a visible smoke that covers mankind as a painful punishment. Commentators are genuinely divided on whether this already occurred, as a famine that struck the Quraysh during the Prophet's lifetime, or is still a coming major sign; both readings exist in the classical tafsir tradition.

references.label: Surah Ad-Dukhan 44:10-11
references.gist: Warns of a day the sky will bring a visible smoke enveloping the people, a painful torment.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2901b
references.gist: The Prophet lists ten signs before the Hour, including the Smoke, Dajjal, and the Beast, as narrated by Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari.

name: Al-Mahdi
summary: Hadith describe a rightly-guided leader from the Prophet's family who will appear before the Hour and fill the earth with justice after it had been filled with oppression. Unlike the prophets or the descent of Isa, the Mahdi is not named in the Quran, and individual narrations about him are graded differently by hadith scholars, from weak to fair, though belief in his coming is widely held.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 4282
references.gist: Describes a man of the Prophet's family, sharing his name and his father's name, who will fill the earth with justice as it had been filled with oppression.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 4284
references.gist: States the Mahdi will be of the Prophet's family, from the descendants of his daughter Fatimah.

name: Ad-Dajjal, the False Messiah
summary: Ad-Dajjal is described in hadith as a man blind in one eye, with the word Kafir, disbeliever, written between his eyes, visible to every believer, who will emerge near the end of days claiming divinity and performing deceptive feats before his defeat.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 7408
references.gist: The Prophet says every prophet before him warned his people of the one-eyed liar, and that Allah, unlike the Dajjal, is not one-eyed.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2901b
references.gist: Names Dajjal among the ten signs before the Hour, in the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari.

name: The Descent of Isa (AS)
summary: Hadith describe Isa ibn Maryam (AS) descending near Damascus to pursue and kill Ad-Dajjal, after which he breaks the cross, ends the jizyah tax, and rules justly, before going on to face Yajuj wa Majuj.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2937a
references.gist: Describes Isa descending near a white minaret east of Damascus, resting his hands on the wings of two angels, then pursuing and killing Ad-Dajjal at the gate of Ludd.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3448
references.gist: The Prophet says Isa will descend as a just ruler, break the cross, kill the pig, and abolish the jizyah tax.

name: Yajuj wa Majuj (Gog and Magog)
summary: The Quran recounts that the righteous ruler Dhul-Qarnayn built a barrier to contain Yajuj and Majuj, a people who caused corruption on the earth, which remains until it is opened by Allah's decree; hadith place their release after the descent of Isa.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:94-99
references.gist: Dhul-Qarnayn builds a barrier of iron and molten copper between two mountains to contain Yajuj and Majuj, which they cannot scale or pierce.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:96
references.gist: States that when Yajuj and Majuj are let loose, they will pour forth from every elevation.

name: Ad-Dabbah, the Beast
summary: The Quran mentions a creature Allah will bring forth from the earth to speak to mankind, marking a moment when the divine decree has come to pass; beyond this verse, its exact nature is not detailed in strongly authenticated narrations.

references.label: Surah An-Naml 27:82
references.gist: Describes a creature brought forth from the earth to speak to people, because mankind lacked certainty in Allah's signs.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2901b
references.gist: Names the Beast (Dabbah) among the ten signs before the Hour.

name: The Sun Rising from the West
summary: Hadith name the sun rising from the west as one of the ten major signs, after which the door of repentance closes; scholars generally regard it as the last of the worldly major signs, occurring very close to the Hour itself.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2901b
references.gist: Names the sun rising from the west among the ten signs before the Hour.

references.label: Surah Al-An'am 6:158
references.gist: Warns that on the day some signs of the Lord arrive, believing will no longer benefit a soul that did not already believe or earn good through its faith.

name: Three Landslides and the Fire
summary: The hadith of Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari names three landslides, in the east, the west, and the Arabian Peninsula, and a fire emerging from the direction of Yemen that drives people to their place of gathering, among the ten signs before the Hour, without fixing a strict order between all ten.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2901b
references.gist: Lists three landslides, in the east, the west, and the Arabian Peninsula, and a fire from Yemen driving people to their gathering place, among the ten signs before the Hour.

name: The Trumpet
summary: The Quran states that the Trumpet will be blown and all in the heavens and earth will fall dead except whom Allah wills, then it will be blown again and all will rise and look on. Tradition commonly names the angel Israfil as the one who blows it, though this rests on general acceptance rather than a text that names him directly.

references.label: Surah Az-Zumar 39:68
references.gist: States the Trumpet will be blown and all in the heavens and earth will fall dead except whom Allah wills, then it will be blown again and they will stand up, looking on.

name: Resurrection and the Gathering
summary: Humanity is resurrected and gathered for reckoning after the Trumpet's blast, each person coming forth with an angel to drive them and an angel to bear witness, their earlier heedlessness removed so their sight becomes sharp that Day.

references.label: Surah Qaf 50:20-22
references.gist: Describes the Trumpet's blast as the promised Day, when every soul comes with a driver and a witness, its earlier heedlessness removed so its sight becomes sharp.

name: Al-Hawd, the Pond
summary: Hadith describe a pond belonging to Muhammad (SAW) at the place of gathering, from which believers will drink before entering Paradise, fed by the river Al-Kawthar granted to him in Paradise.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6576
references.gist: Describes the Prophet's pond (Al-Hawd), and his statement that some who had claimed to follow him will be turned away from it for introducing innovations or turning back after he left them, a sober warning rather than a blanket assurance.

name: Ash-Shafa'ah, the Intercession
summary: Believers will seek someone to intercede with Allah on their behalf, going in turn to Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, and Isa, each of whom declines and points them to the next, until they reach Muhammad (SAW), who is granted this intercession as one of his distinguishing honors on that Day.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4712
references.gist: Describes people going to Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, and Isa in turn seeking intercession, each declining and pointing to the next, until Muhammad prostrates before the Throne and is granted the greater intercession.

name: Al-Mizan, the Scale
summary: The Quran states that Allah will set up scales of justice for the Day of Judgment so that no soul is wronged in the slightest, weighing even a deed the weight of a mustard seed.

references.label: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:47
references.gist: States Allah will set up just scales for the Day of Resurrection so no soul is wronged, weighing even a deed the weight of a mustard seed.

references.label: Surah Al-Qari'ah 101:6-9
references.gist: States whoever's scale is heavy with good deeds will be in a pleasant life, while whoever's scale is light will have their abode in the abyss.

name: Categories of People on the Day of Judgment
summary: The Quran describes more than one way people are divided that Day: some receive their record in their right hand and rejoice, others receive it in their left hand or behind their back in despair, and Surah Al-Waqi'ah divides mankind into three ultimate classes.

references.label: Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:7-10
references.gist: States that on that Day people will be sorted into three classes: the companions of the right, the companions of the left, and the foremost, who are nearest to Allah.

references.label: Surah Al-Haqqah 69:19
references.gist: Whoever is given their record in their right hand will say, 'Here, read my record.'

references.label: Surah Al-Haqqah 69:25
references.gist: Whoever is given their record in their left hand will wish they had never been given it.

references.label: Surah Al-Inshiqaq 84:7
references.gist: One given his record in his right hand will have an easy reckoning.

references.label: Surah Al-Inshiqaq 84:10
references.gist: One given his record behind his back will call out for destruction.

references.label: Surah Ali 'Imran 3:106-107
references.gist: Describes some faces turning white and some turning black on that Day; the blackened are asked whether they disbelieved after having believed, and the whitened are received into Allah's mercy.

name: The Believers' Light
summary: The Quran describes believers moving toward Paradise that Day with a light running ahead of them and in their right hands, while hypocrites who ask to share it are told to go back and seek their own; a wall with a gate is raised between them, mercy on one side, torment on the other.

references.label: Surah Al-Hadid 57:12
references.gist: Describes believing men and women with their light running before them and in their right hands that Day, given the glad tidings of gardens beneath which rivers flow.

references.label: Surah Al-Hadid 57:13
references.gist: Hypocrites ask the believers to wait so they can share their light; told to go back and seek their own, a wall is put up between them with a gate, mercy inside it and torment outside.

name: As-Sirat, the Bridge
summary: Hadith describe a bridge laid across Hell that every person must cross, thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword, fitted with hooks that seize people according to their deeds.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6573
references.gist: Describes the bridge (As-Sirat) laid across Hell, with hooks that seize people according to their deeds, and states the Prophet will be the first to cross it.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 183b
references.gist: Describes believers crossing the bridge at different speeds, some safely, some lacerated, some falling into the Fire below, in proportion to their deeds.

name: Jannah and Jahannam
summary: These are the two final abodes to which every soul is sent once judgment is complete: Paradise, an eternal dwelling promised to those who believed and did righteous deeds, and Hell, a fire whose inhabitants are driven back whenever they try to escape.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:25
references.gist: Describes Paradise as gardens beneath which rivers flow, given to those who believed and did righteous deeds, abiding there forever with pure spouses.

references.label: Surah Al-Hajj 22:19-22
references.gist: Describes Hell's inhabitants fitted with garments of fire, boiling water poured over their heads, and driven back with hooked rods of iron whenever they try to escape it.

name: Deeds and Their Outcomes
summary: The Quran and hadith tie specific deeds to specific outcomes rather than leaving the connection abstract. These are illustrative examples, not an exhaustive list of every deed and its consequence.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2589
references.gist: Defines backbiting (ghibah) as saying something true about your brother that he would dislike being said; saying something false about him instead is slander.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 4878
references.gist: The Prophet describes seeing, during his ascent to heaven, people with copper nails scratching their own faces and chests; Jibril identifies them as those who backbit others and violated their honor in worldly life.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 660
references.gist: Names seven whom Allah will shade on the Day when there is no shade but His, including a youth who grew up devoted to Allah's worship, a just ruler, and one who gives charity so secretly his left hand does not know what his right has given.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:114
references.gist: States that good deeds remove the effects of bad deeds.

name: The Five Pillars of Islam
summary: The Prophet structured Islam into five obligations in a single hadith.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 8
references.gist: Islam is built on five: testimony of faith, prayer, zakat, fasting Ramadan, and Hajj for those able.

name: Shahada: The Declaration of Faith
summary: The declaration that there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His Messenger.

references.label: Surah Aal-Imran 3:18
references.gist: Allah bears witness there is no god but Him, and so do the angels and people of knowledge.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 8
references.gist: Names the testimony of faith as the first of the five pillars.

name: Salah: The Five Daily Prayers
summary: The five daily prayers. The Quran commands prayer at set times; the number of prayers, their rak'ah counts, and their physical form come from hadith.

references.label: Surah Hud 11:114
references.gist: Commands establishing prayer at the two ends of the day and the approach of the night.

references.label: Surah Al-Isra 17:78
references.gist: Commands prayer from the decline of the sun until nightfall, and the recitation of dawn.

references.label: Surah An-Nur 24:58
references.gist: Names Fajr and Isha directly (salat al-fajr, salat al-isha).

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:238
references.gist: Commands guarding the prayers and 'the middle prayer' (al-wusta), without naming it.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 349
references.gist: The Mi'raj hadith: prayer is fixed at five times daily after being reduced from fifty, still counted as fifty in reward.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 350
references.gist: Prayer was first prescribed as two rak'ahs at a time; two more were later added for those not traveling, and Maghrib is not shortened while traveling.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 612a
references.gist: Gives the time window for each of the five prayers in turn, naming Fajr, Zuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha directly.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 627a
references.gist: The Prophet names the Quran's unnamed 'middle prayer' as Asr, after the Muslims were kept from it during the Battle of the Trench.

sections.heading: How to Pray
sections.intro: The obligation and the rak'ah counts come from the references above; the physical steps of prayer itself come from these two hadith.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 757
references.gist: The Prophet teaches a man the physical steps of prayer, takbir, recitation, bowing, rising, prostrating, after correcting him three times for praying badly.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 631
references.gist: 'Pray as you have seen me praying.'

name: Zakat: Obligatory Almsgiving
summary: Obligatory almsgiving, paired with prayer throughout the Quran.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:43
references.gist: Commands establishing prayer and giving zakat together.

references.label: Surah At-Tawbah 9:60
references.gist: Names the eight categories of people entitled to receive zakat.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1454
references.gist: Abu Bakr's written zakat instruction, with exact livestock rates and thresholds.

name: Sawm: Fasting Ramadan
summary: Fasting the month of Ramadan.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:183-187
references.gist: Prescribes fasting for believers as it was prescribed for those before them, and sets Ramadan as the fixed period.

name: Hajj: Pilgrimage to the House
summary: Pilgrimage to the House in Makkah.

references.label: Surah Aal-Imran 3:97
references.gist: States pilgrimage is owed to Allah by whoever is able to find a way there.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:196-203
references.gist: Details the rites of Hajj.

references.label: Jami at-Tirmidhi 889
references.gist: 'The Hajj is Arafah': standing at Arafah is what most fundamentally constitutes a valid Hajj.

name: Iman: The Six Articles of Faith
summary: The foundational hadith distinguishing Islam, Iman, and Ihsan, and the source for the six articles of faith covered individually below.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 50
references.gist: Narrates Jibril's appearance in human form and his three-part question to the Prophet on Islam, Iman, and Ihsan.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 8a
references.gist: Muslim's version of the same encounter, with the same six-part definition of Iman.

name: Belief in Allah
summary: The first article of faith: Allah's oneness (tawhid).

references.label: Surah Al-Ikhlas 112
references.gist: The Quran's most concentrated single statement of Allah's oneness, self-sufficiency, and incomparability.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 5015
references.gist: The Prophet says Surah Al-Ikhlas is equal in weight to a third of the Quran.

references.label: Ayat al-Kursi, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:255
references.gist: Declares there is no god but Allah, the Ever-Living, sustaining all existence.

name: Belief in the Angels
summary: The second article of faith: belief in the existence of Allah's angels. Covered in depth under Cosmology.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:285
references.gist: States that the Messenger and the believers believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.

name: Belief in the Books
summary: The third article of faith: belief that Allah revealed scriptures to His prophets.

references.label: Surah Al-Ala 87:19
references.gist: Names the Suhuf, scrolls given to Ibrahim, as an earlier revelation.

references.label: Surah An-Najm 53:36-37
references.gist: Names the Suhuf of Ibrahim and Musa together.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:44
references.gist: States the Tawrah was sent down to Musa with guidance and light.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:46
references.gist: States Isa was given the Injil, confirming what came before it.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:163
references.gist: States the Zabur was given to Dawud.

references.label: Surah Al-Hijr 15:9
references.gist: Allah states He sent down the message (the Quran) and will preserve it.

name: Belief in the Messengers
summary: The fourth article of faith: belief in all of Allah's messengers without distinction between them. Each is covered individually in the Tree view. This is a matter of believing in them equally, not a claim that every prophet held the same role; see Nabi and Rasul for that distinction.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:136
references.gist: Believers declare they make no distinction between any of Allah's messengers.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:285
references.gist: Restates the same principle of not distinguishing between messengers.

name: Nabi and Rasul
summary: The Quran treats 'nabi' (prophet) and 'rasul' (messenger) as two distinct terms rather than pure synonyms, naming them separately in the same breath. Scholars commonly explain a rasul as one sent with a new law or scripture to a people, while a nabi may reaffirm an existing one without necessarily bringing something new; every rasul is also a nabi, but not every nabi is necessarily a rasul. This is a terminological distinction, not a ranking of who deserves belief; see Belief in the Messengers for that.

references.label: Surah Al-Hajj 22:52
references.gist: States that Allah did not send any rasul (messenger) or nabi (prophet) before the Prophet without Satan interfering in his wishes, naming the two as distinct categories in the same breath.

references.label: Surah Maryam 19:51
references.gist: Calls Musa both a rasul (messenger) and a nabi (prophet) in the same verse, showing a rasul is also a nabi.

name: Belief in the Last Day
summary: The fifth article of faith: belief in the Day of Judgment. Covered in full sequence under End Times.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:177
references.gist: Names belief in the Last Day alongside belief in Allah as a core criterion of true righteousness.

name: Belief in Divine Decree (Qadar)
summary: The sixth article of faith: belief in Divine Decree, its good and its bad.

references.label: Surah Al-Qamar 54:49
references.gist: States Allah created all things with predestination.

references.label: Jami at-Tirmidhi 2144
references.gist: A slave does not truly believe until he believes that what struck him could not have missed him, and what missed him could not have struck him.

name: Rights of Parents
summary: Kindness to parents, commanded in the same breath as the worship of Allah alone.

references.label: Surah Al-Isra 17:23-24
references.gist: Forbids even the mildest word of contempt toward parents and commands a humble tone toward them in old age.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 5971
references.gist: The Prophet names 'your mother' three times before 'your father' when asked who most deserves good companionship.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2548
references.gist: Muslim's version of the same hadith on mother and father.

name: Rights of Neighbors
summary: The Prophet placed heavy emphasis on treating neighbors well.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6014
references.gist: Jibril kept advising the Prophet about the neighbor's right until he thought a neighbor would inherit.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 2624
references.gist: Muslim's version of the same hadith on the neighbor's right.

name: Rights of Animals
summary: Islam extends real accountability to how animals are treated, even ones a person has no other duty toward. The Prophet taught that a woman was punished in Hell for locking a cat up without feeding it or letting it hunt for itself, while a man was forgiven all his sins for climbing down a well to fetch water in his shoe for a dog dying of thirst, and confirmed there is reward in kindness to every living creature.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 3318
references.gist: Ibn Umar narrates the Prophet said a woman was tormented in Hell because of a cat she had tied up, neither feeding it nor releasing it to hunt for itself.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 2466
references.gist: Abu Hurairah narrates a man gave water to a thirsty dog by filling his shoe from a well, and Allah forgave him; the Prophet confirmed there is a reward for kindness to every living creature.

name: Rights of Guests
summary: The Prophet tied honoring a guest directly to faith itself, in the same breath as not harming one's neighbor and speaking only good or staying silent, three markers he gave of what believing in Allah and the Last Day actually looks like in practice.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018
references.gist: Abu Hurairah narrates the Prophet said whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should not harm his neighbor, should honor his guest, and should speak good or remain silent.

name: Rights of Spouses
summary: The rights owed between husband and wife.

references.label: Surah Ar-Rum 30:21
references.gist: Describes spouses as a source of mutual tranquility and affection.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:19
references.gist: Commands husbands to live with their wives in kindness.

references.label: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3895
references.gist: The best among believers is the one best to his family; the Prophet says he was the best to his family.

name: Rights of Orphans
summary: The Quran is unusually direct about the rights of orphans.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:10
references.gist: Those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly are, in effect, swallowing fire.

references.label: Surah Ad-Duha 93:9
references.gist: Commands: do not oppress the orphan.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6005
references.gist: The Prophet and the caretaker of an orphan will be together in Paradise like two joined fingers.

name: Rights of Children
summary: The Quran forbids killing children out of fear of poverty, stating Allah provides for both them and their parents, and calling it a grave sin. The Prophet required fathers to be just between their children in gifts, refusing to witness one man favoring a single son, and taught that showing them physical affection is a mark of mercy: whoever shows no mercy will be shown none.

references.label: Surah Al-Isra 17:31
references.gist: Forbids killing children out of fear of poverty, since Allah provides for them and their parents, calling it a grave sin.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 2587
references.gist: The Prophet refuses to witness a father giving a gift to only one son, telling him to fear Allah and be just between his children.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 5997
references.gist: The Prophet kisses his grandson; told a man never kisses his own children, he replies that whoever shows no mercy will be shown none.

name: The Sanctity of Life, Property, and Honor
summary: From the Farewell Sermon (see the Farewell Pilgrimage entry for the event itself).

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1739
references.gist: Declares the blood, property, and honor of every believer sacred to one another, like the sanctity of that day.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 1218a
references.gist: Muslim's version of the same Farewell Sermon declaration.

name: Rights of the Poor and Needy
summary: Neglecting the poor is treated as a sign of hollow faith, distinct from Zakat's fixed obligation.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'un 107:1-7
references.gist: Al-Ma'un ties denial of the Day of Judgment to repelling the orphan and not urging that the poor be fed.

name: Human Equality and Dignity
summary: Also from the Farewell Sermon.

references.label: Musnad Ahmad 22978
references.gist: No Arab has superiority over a non-Arab, nor any race over another, except through piety.

name: Riba (Usury and Interest)
summary: Usury and interest are prohibited in strong terms.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:278-279
references.gist: Commands giving up remaining riba, warning of war against Allah and His Messenger for those who persist.

references.label: Surah Aal-Imran 3:130
references.gist: Commands not consuming riba 'doubled and multiplied.'

name: Intoxicants and Gambling
summary: The prohibition of intoxicants and gambling came in three stages.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:219
references.gist: First stage: acknowledges some benefit in intoxicants and gambling, but states their sin is greater.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:43
references.gist: Second stage: forbids approaching prayer while intoxicated.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:90-91
references.gist: Final stage: calls intoxicants and gambling an abomination of Satan's handiwork and commands believers to shun them.

name: Zina (Unlawful Sexual Relations)
summary: Unlawful sexual relations, with an unusually demanding evidentiary standard in classical law.

references.label: Surah Al-Isra 17:32
references.gist: Commands not even approaching zina, calling it an indecency and an evil way.

references.label: Surah An-Nur 24:2
references.gist: Sets a hundred lashes for the unmarried offender before witnesses; classical law requires four eyewitnesses to the act itself.

name: Forbidden Foods
summary: The Quran's dietary prohibitions.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:173
references.gist: Forbids carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of other than Allah.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:3
references.gist: Repeats the same core list and adds detail on animals killed by strangling, a blow, a fall, or goring.

name: Inheritance Shares
summary: The Quran states specific inheritance shares with real numeric precision; this is a simplified summary of the primary verses only, classical inheritance law has further rules not covered here.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:11-12
references.gist: Sets shares for children, parents, and spouses, e.g. a son receives twice a daughter's share.

name: The Seven Destructive Sins
summary: A hadith naming seven sins the Prophet called destructive.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 2766
references.gist: Lists shirk, sorcery, unjust killing, riba, consuming an orphan's wealth, fleeing battle, and slandering chaste believing women.

name: Honesty in Trade
summary: A foundational hadith on commercial honesty.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 102
references.gist: The Prophet finds wet grain hidden under dry grain and says: 'whoever deceives us is not of us.'

name: Wudu (Ablution)
summary: The ritual washing required before prayer, one of the few ritual procedures the Quran states directly, step by step.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:6
references.gist: States the actual steps: wash the face, wash the hands and arms to the elbows, wipe the head, wash the feet to the ankles.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 244
references.gist: Washing the face, hands, and feet in wudu washes away the sins committed by those body parts, until one emerges pure.

name: Ghusl (Ritual Bath)
summary: The full-body ritual bath required after major impurity (janabah), commanded in the same verse as wudu and tayammum.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:6
references.gist: Commands: 'if you are in a state of janabah, then purify yourselves,' the same verse that describes wudu.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 248
references.gist: Describes the Prophet's own ghusl: washing the hands, performing wudu, working water through the hair roots, then pouring water over the head and body.

name: Tayammum (Dry Ablution)
summary: Purification with clean earth when water is unavailable or cannot be used, a concession named directly in the Quran.

references.label: Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:6
references.gist: Permits tayammum with clean earth, wiping the face and hands, for the ill, traveling, or without water.

references.label: Surah An-Nisa 4:43
references.gist: States the same permission for tayammum in illness, travel, after relieving oneself, or after intimacy, when no water is found.

name: The Adhan (Call to Prayer)
summary: The call to prayer, whose wording was revealed through a companion's dream and confirmed by the Prophet.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 499
references.gist: Abdullah ibn Zayd dreams the wording of the Adhan; the Prophet confirms it as a true vision and has Bilal call it, for his louder voice.

name: Jumu'ah (Friday Prayer)
summary: The congregational Friday prayer, commanded directly in its own named Quran surah.

references.label: Surah Al-Jumu'ah 62:9
references.gist: Commands believers to hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade when the call to Friday prayer is made.

name: Funeral Prayer (Salat al-Janazah)
summary: The prayer offered for a deceased Muslim, one of the five rights a Muslim owes another.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1240
references.gist: Lists following the funeral procession among the five rights a Muslim owes another Muslim.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1325
references.gist: Whoever attends until the funeral prayer earns one qirat of reward; whoever stays until burial earns two, each like a huge mountain.

name: Sayyid al-Istighfar (The Master Supplication for Forgiveness)
summary: The Prophet called this the best way to seek Allah's forgiveness: whoever says it during the day with sure faith in it and dies that day, or says it at night and dies before morning, enters Paradise.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6306
references.gist: Shaddad ibn Aws narrates the Prophet taught 'Allahumma anta rabbi la ilaha illa anta, khalaqtani wa ana abduka...' (O Allah, You are my Lord, none has the right to be worshipped except You, You created me and I am Your servant), acknowledging Allah's favor and one's own sin and asking forgiveness, calling it the master of all supplications for forgiveness.

name: Morning and Evening Protection Dua (Three Times)
summary: A short daily protection formula the Prophet taught to be said three times each morning and three times each evening, invoking Allah's name against harm.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 5088
references.gist: Uthman ibn Affan reports the Prophet said whoever says 'Bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru ma'as-mihi shay'un fil-ardi wa la fis-sama'i wa huwas-Sami'ul-Alim' (In the name of Allah, with whose name nothing on earth or in heaven can cause harm, and He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing) three times each morning and evening will not be harmed by anything that day or night.

references.label: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3388
references.gist: A parallel narration of the same protection formula and promise, also from Uthman ibn Affan, graded hasan sahih by at-Tirmidhi.

name: Ayat al-Kursi Before Sleep for Protection
summary: Reciting Ayat al-Kursi (Quran 2:255) upon going to bed is authentically reported to bring a protector from Allah against Satan until morning.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 2311
references.gist: Abu Hurairah narrates that a jinn caught stealing from charity food taught him to recite Ayat al-Kursi upon going to bed so that Allah would appoint a guard and no devil would come near until morning; the Prophet confirmed this was true even though the jinn was, in Abu Hurairah's words, an absolute liar.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:255 (Ayat al-Kursi)
references.gist: The Throne Verse itself, describing Allah's living, sustaining, all-encompassing knowledge and dominion, the verse specified in the hadith above for nightly recitation.

name: Dua Before Eating
summary: Saying Bismillah before eating and using the right hand, eating from what is nearest, is a direct instruction of the Prophet to a young boy at his table.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 5376
references.gist: Umar ibn Abi Salama narrates the Prophet told him as a boy: 'Say Bismillah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is nearer to you.'

name: Dua After Eating
summary: A short dua of thanks the Prophet would say upon finishing a meal.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 3850
references.gist: Reports that when the Prophet finished eating he said 'Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi at'amani hadha, wa razaqanihi min ghayri hawlin minni wa la quwwah' (Praise be to Allah who fed me this and provided it for me without any might or power on my part).

name: Dua for Entering the Home
summary: A dua asking Allah for the best outcome of entering and leaving, said before greeting one's family with salam. Its chain is graded differently by hadith scholars, weak by al-Albani and hasan by Ibn Baz, so treat it as well known but less firmly established than the other duas here.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 5096
references.gist: Abu Malik al-Ash'ari narrates that on entering his house a man should say 'Allahumma inni as'aluka khayral-mawliji wa khayral-makhraji...' (O Allah, I ask You for the best entrance and the best exit, in Allah's name we enter and in Allah's name we leave, and upon our Lord we place our trust), then greet the household with salam.

name: Dua for Leaving the Home
summary: A short, well-authenticated dua said when stepping out of the house, after which the Prophet said the person is guided, protected, and defended from Satan.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 5095
references.gist: Anas ibn Malik reports the Prophet said whoever, on leaving his house, says 'Bismillahi tawakkaltu 'ala Allah, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah' (In the name of Allah, I place my trust in Allah, there is no power and no strength except with Allah) will be told 'you are guided, defended, and protected,' and the devils will turn away from him.

references.label: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3426
references.gist: The same narration and wording via Anas ibn Malik, graded hasan sahih by at-Tirmidhi.

name: Dua for Entering the Masjid
summary: A short dua asking for Allah's mercy, said upon stepping into the mosque.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 713
references.gist: Narrates the Prophet said that on entering the mosque one should say 'Allahummaf-tah li abwaba rahmatik' (O Allah, open the gates of Your mercy for me).

name: Dua for Leaving the Masjid
summary: The companion dua to the entering-masjid supplication, said when leaving, asking for Allah's bounty in the world outside.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 713
references.gist: The same hadith as the entering-masjid dua: on leaving the mosque one should say 'Allahumma inni as'aluka min fadlika' (O Allah, I ask You for Your bounty).

name: Dua Before Sleeping
summary: The Prophet's regular final words before going to sleep, entrusting his life and death to Allah.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6324
references.gist: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman narrates that whenever the Prophet went to bed he would say 'Bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya' (In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live).

name: Dua Upon Waking Up
summary: The matching dua of praise said immediately upon waking, thanking Allah for the return to life that sleep represents.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6312
references.gist: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman reports that when the Prophet woke up he would say 'Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur' (All praise is for Allah who gave us life after having caused us to die, and unto Him is the resurrection).

name: Dua for Times of Distress
summary: A dua of pure declaration of Allah's greatness that the Prophet would recite specifically when facing distress or a crisis.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6346
references.gist: Ibn Abbas narrates the Prophet used to say at a time of distress 'La ilaha illallahul-Azimul-Halim, la ilaha illallahu Rabbul-Arshil-Azim, la ilaha illallahu Rabbus-samawati wa Rabbul-ardi wa Rabbul-Arshil-Karim' (None has the right to be worshipped but Allah, the Great, the Forbearing; none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, Lord of the Magnificent Throne; none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, Lord of the heavens, the earth, and the Noble Throne).

name: Seeking Forgiveness (Istighfar) Regularly
summary: Simply saying 'Astaghfirullah' (I seek Allah's forgiveness) is a practice the Prophet himself performed many times a day, establishing it as a general daily habit rather than tied to a single occasion.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6307
references.gist: Abu Hurairah reports the Prophet said: 'By Allah, I seek Allah's forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance more than seventy times a day.'

name: Dua for Entering the Bathroom
summary: A dua seeking Allah's protection from harmful unseen beings, said before entering the toilet area.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 142
references.gist: Anas ibn Malik reports that when the Prophet entered the toilet he would say 'Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-khubthi wal-khaba'ith' (O Allah, I seek refuge in You from male and female devils).

references.label: Sahih Muslim 375
references.gist: A parallel narration of the same dua and occasion, agreed upon by Bukhari and Muslim.

name: Dua for Leaving the Bathroom
summary: A single short dua of seeking forgiveness said by the Prophet upon exiting the toilet.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 30
references.gist: Aisha reports that when the Prophet came out of the toilet he would say 'Ghufranak' (I seek Your forgiveness).

references.label: Jami at-Tirmidhi 7
references.gist: A parallel narration of the same short dua, 'Ghufranak,' from Aisha upon leaving the toilet.

name: Dua When It Rains
summary: A short dua asking Allah to make the rain beneficial, said by the Prophet upon seeing rainfall.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1032
references.gist: Aisha reports that when the Prophet saw rain he would say 'Allahumma sayyiban nafi'an' (O Allah, make it a beneficial rain cloud).

name: Dua for a Sick Person
summary: A specific short dua the Prophet instructed be said seven times over a sick person whose time of death has not yet come.

references.label: Sunan Abi Dawud 3106
references.gist: Ibn Abbas narrates the Prophet said whoever visits a sick person whose time has not come and says seven times 'As'alu Allahal-Azima Rabbal-Arshil-Azimi an yashfiyak' (I ask Allah the Mighty, Lord of the Mighty Throne, to cure you), Allah will cure him of that illness.

references.label: Jami at-Tirmidhi 2083
references.gist: A parallel narration of the same dua and instruction to repeat it seven times when visiting the sick.

name: The Traveler's Dua
summary: A dua said when setting out on a journey, combining takbir, a Quranic verse of gratitude for one's means of transport, and requests for a safe, easy trip.

references.label: Sahih Muslim 1342
references.gist: Ibn Umar reports that when the Prophet mounted his ride to set out on a journey he would say 'Allahu Akbar' three times, then a Quranic verse of gratitude for being granted this means of travel, followed by asking Allah for righteousness, piety, and an easy journey, and seeking refuge from hardship and bad outcomes on return.

name: Dua for One's Parents
summary: A Quranic dua that Allah Himself instructs children to say for their parents, asking for mercy upon them in return for the mercy they showed while raising the child.

references.label: Surah Al-Isra 17:24
references.gist: 'Rabbi irhamhuma kama rabbayani saghira' (My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small), part of a passage (17:23-24) commanding kindness, humility, and mercy toward one's parents.

name: Dua for Anxiety and Grief
summary: A comprehensive dua the Prophet taught seeking refuge from anxiety, sorrow, weakness, laziness, debt, and being overpowered by others.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6369
references.gist: Anas ibn Malik narrates the Prophet used to say 'Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan, wal-'ajzi wal-kasal, wal-bukhli wal-jubn, wa dala'id-dayni wa ghalabatir-rijal' (O Allah, I seek refuge in You from anxiety and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from miserliness and cowardice, from being overcome by debt and being overpowered by others).

name: Dua for Ease When Facing Difficulty
summary: A short dua affirming that nothing is easy except what Allah makes easy, said when a matter becomes hard for a person.

references.label: Sahih Ibn Hibban 2427
references.gist: Anas ibn Malik narrates the Prophet said 'Allahumma la sahla illa ma ja'altahu sahla, wa anta taj'alul-hazna idha shi'ta sahla' (O Allah, there is no ease except in that which You have made easy, and You make the difficult, if You wish, easy), graded sahih by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani and al-Albani.

name: Dua After the Adhan
summary: A dua said after hearing the call to prayer, asking Allah to grant Muhammad (SAW) the station of intercession, in return for which the Prophet promised his intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 614
references.gist: Jabir ibn Abdullah narrates the Prophet said whoever, after hearing the adhan, says 'Allahumma Rabba hadhihid-da'watit-tammah...' (O Allah, Lord of this perfect call and of the prayer about to be established, grant Muhammad the wasilah and excellence, and raise him to the praiseworthy station You promised him), will be granted the Prophet's intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

name: What to Say When Someone Sneezes
summary: A short exchange the Prophet taught between a person who sneezes and those around them.

references.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6224
references.gist: Abu Hurairah narrates the Prophet said: if anyone sneezes he should say 'Alhamdulillah,' and whoever hears it should reply 'Yarhamuk Allah' (may Allah have mercy on you), to which the sneezer should reply 'Yahdikumullah wa yuslih balakum' (may Allah guide you and set your condition right).

name: The People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf)
summary: A group of young believers fled a people who demanded they worship other than Allah, took refuge in a cave, and were put into a long sleep for years before being awakened as a sign to those who found them.

provenDates.label: 309 years asleep in the cave, though the very next verse adds that Allah knows best

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:25-26
references.gist: States they remained three hundred years, plus nine, then immediately says Allah knows best how long they stayed.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:9-26
references.gist: The full account: youths flee to a cave, are put to sleep for a long span of years, and are eventually found, with the exact number of years left uncertain except that Allah knows best.

tale.intro: The account opens as Allah poses it to the Prophet (SAW) as a sign worth reflecting on.

chapters.heading: A Sign Among Signs
chapters.narrative: Allah asks whether the companions of the cave and 'the inscription' were a wonder among His other signs. The youths retreated to the cave and prayed, 'Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us right guidance in our affair.' Allah then cast a cover of sleep over their ears within the cave for a number of years, so that He might later show which of two disputing factions had most precisely reckoned how long they had remained.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:9-12
references.gist: The youths retreat to the cave, pray for mercy and guidance, and are put to sleep for a span of years so it can later be shown which faction reckoned the time most precisely.

chapters.heading: Youths Who Stood for Their Lord
chapters.narrative: Allah relates their story in truth: they were youths who believed in their Lord, and He increased them in guidance. He strengthened their hearts when they stood and proclaimed, 'Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; never will we invoke besides Him any deity.' They observed that their own people had taken other gods without clear authority, and said to one another that since they had withdrawn from their people and what they worshipped besides Allah, they should retreat to the cave, where their Lord would spread His mercy over them and ease their affair.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:13-16
references.gist: They were youths who believed in their Lord, publicly rejected the gods of their people, and withdrew to the cave to seek Allah's mercy and ease.

chapters.heading: Asleep Under Allah's Watch
chapters.narrative: Had one been present, one would have seen the sun incline away from their cave to the right as it rose and pass them on the left as it set, while they lay in its open space - a sign from Allah. They appeared awake though they were asleep, and Allah turned them from side to side, while their dog stretched its forelegs at the entrance. Had anyone looked upon them, they would have fled from them in terror.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:17-18
references.gist: The sun's movement around the cave, the sleepers being turned from side to side, and their dog stretched out at the entrance are described as signs from Allah.

chapters.heading: Waking, and the Errand for Food
chapters.narrative: When they were raised up, they questioned one another about how long they had remained; some said a day or part of a day, then agreed that their Lord knew best. They sent one of them to the city with their silver coin to find the best food and bring back provision, cautioning him to be careful and let no one become aware of them - for if their people found them, they would be stoned or forced back to their former religion, and they would never succeed again.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:19-20
references.gist: Upon waking they debate how long they slept, then send one of them into the city with a silver coin to buy food discreetly, warned of the danger if their people discover them.

chapters.heading: Found, and a Dispute Over Their Number
chapters.narrative: Allah caused them to be discovered so that people would know His promise is true and the Hour is beyond doubt. Those who found them disputed over what to do, some saying a structure should be built over them, with 'their Lord is most knowing about them,' while those who prevailed said they would take a place of worship over them. Later, people would guess at their number - three, with a fourth their dog; five, with a sixth their dog; or seven, with an eighth their dog - all 'guessing at the unseen.' The Quran instructs: say that Allah is most knowing of their number, that only a few truly know it, and not to argue about them except with clear knowledge.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:21-22
references.gist: The people who find them dispute over what to build over them; later generations dispute their number, which the Quran says only Allah truly knows.

chapters.heading: How Long They Remained
chapters.narrative: The Quran states that they remained in their cave three hundred years, and adds nine more - but then immediately instructs: 'Say, Allah is most knowing of how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth; how Seeing is He and how Hearing.' The figure is given, and in the same breath the matter is returned to Allah's knowledge alone.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:25-26
references.gist: States they remained three hundred years plus nine, then immediately says Allah alone truly knows how long they remained.

name: Dhul-Qarnayn
summary: A powerful ruler whom Allah established on the earth and gave the means to travel far to the west and east, dealing justly with the peoples he met and eventually building a barrier to contain Gog and Magog; the Quran does not name who he historically was.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:83-98
references.gist: In answer to a question about Dhul-Qarnayn, the Quran describes his journeys to the west and east and his building of a barrier against Gog and Magog.

tale.intro: The Quran does not identify Dhul-Qarnayn with any specific historical king; scholars have long debated who he was, and that identity is left unstated here rather than asserted as fact.

chapters.heading: A Ruler Given Great Means
chapters.narrative: The Prophet (SAW) was asked about Dhul-Qarnayn and told to say he would recite a report about him. Allah had established him firmly on the earth and given him a way to everything he sought, so he followed a way.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:83-85
references.gist: Allah established Dhul-Qarnayn on the earth and gave him the means to pursue whatever he set out to do.

chapters.heading: Journey to the West
chapters.narrative: He journeyed until he reached the setting of the sun, finding it, as it appeared to him, setting into a spring of dark mud, and he found a people there. Allah told him he could either punish them or treat them with goodness. He answered that whoever did wrong would be punished, then returned to his Lord who would give him a terrible punishment, but whoever believed and did righteousness would have the reward of Paradise, and Dhul-Qarnayn would deal with him with ease.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:86-88
references.gist: At the westernmost point of his journey he finds a people and is given the choice to punish or treat them well; he sets out a just principle for how he will deal with wrongdoers and believers.

chapters.heading: Journey to the East
chapters.narrative: He followed another way until he reached the rising of the sun, finding it rising upon a people for whom Allah had made no shelter against it. The Quran adds that Allah's knowledge fully encompassed what Dhul-Qarnayn possessed.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:89-91
references.gist: At the easternmost point of his journey he finds a people exposed with no shelter from the sun; Allah's knowledge encompassed all that Dhul-Qarnayn had.

chapters.heading: A People Threatened by Corruption
chapters.narrative: He followed still another way until, between two mountains, he found a people who could barely understand speech. They told him that Gog and Magog were spreading corruption in the land, and asked whether they might pay him to build a barrier between them. He answered that what his Lord had established him in was better than their payment, but asked them to assist him with labor, and he would build a barrier between them.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:92-95
references.gist: A people between two mountains ask Dhul-Qarnayn for protection from the corruption of Gog and Magog; he declines payment but asks for their labor to build a barrier.

chapters.heading: The Barrier
chapters.narrative: Dhul-Qarnayn had them bring him sheets of iron until he had leveled the gap between the two mountainsides, then had them blow on it until it was like fire, and poured molten copper over it. Gog and Magog were then unable to climb over it or pierce through it. He said this was a mercy from his Lord, but that when his Lord's promise came, He would level it, for His promise is always true. This barrier and the eventual release of Gog and Magog are covered in fuller depth in this site's End Times entry on Yajuj wa Majuj; this account focuses on Dhul-Qarnayn himself.

references.label: Surah Al-Kahf 18:96-98
references.gist: Dhul-Qarnayn builds a barrier of iron and molten copper that Gog and Magog cannot climb or pierce, calling it a mercy from his Lord that will one day be leveled by Allah's promise.

name: Luqman
summary: A man given wisdom by Allah, remembered chiefly for the counsel he gave his son, covering the gravity of shirk, Allah's total knowledge, worship, good character, and humility.

references.label: Surah Luqman 31:12-19
references.gist: Allah gave Luqman wisdom, and this passage records the advice he gave his son on faith, worship, and character.

tale.intro: The Quran gives no genealogy or biography for Luqman beyond calling him a man granted wisdom; what is preserved here is his counsel.

chapters.heading: Wisdom and Gratitude
chapters.narrative: Allah gave Luqman wisdom, telling him to be grateful, for whoever is grateful is grateful for his own benefit, while whoever denies His favor should know Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.

references.label: Surah Luqman 31:12
references.gist: Allah granted Luqman wisdom and told him to be grateful, since gratitude benefits the grateful person themselves.

chapters.heading: The First Warning: Do Not Associate Partners with Allah
chapters.narrative: While instructing his son, Luqman told him, 'O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association with Him is a great injustice.'

references.label: Surah Luqman 31:13
references.gist: Luqman's opening advice to his son is a direct warning against shirk, calling it a great injustice.

chapters.heading: A Word About Parents
chapters.narrative: Immediately after this, the passage turns to Allah's own instruction to mankind about parents - that a mother carries her child in weakness upon weakness and weans him within two years, and that one should be grateful to Allah and to one's parents, though not to the point of obeying them into shirk; even then, one should still accompany them in this world with kindness. This portion is addressed by Allah directly rather than framed as Luqman's own words to his son, but it sits within the same passage.

references.label: Surah Luqman 31:14-15
references.gist: Allah instructs gratitude and kindness toward parents even while forbidding obedience to them in shirk.

chapters.heading: Allah Knows Even a Grain Hidden in a Rock
chapters.narrative: Luqman told his son that if a wrong were the weight of a mustard seed, and were hidden inside a rock or anywhere in the heavens or the earth, Allah would bring it forth, for Allah is Subtle and Acquainted with all things.

references.label: Surah Luqman 31:16
references.gist: Luqman teaches that nothing is hidden from Allah, not even something as small as a mustard seed inside a rock.

chapters.heading: Prayer, Right and Wrong, and Patience
chapters.narrative: He told his son to establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently whatever befalls him, for this is among the matters requiring real resolve.

references.label: Surah Luqman 31:17
references.gist: Luqman instructs his son to pray, command good, forbid wrong, and be patient through hardship.

chapters.heading: Humility in Bearing and Speech
chapters.narrative: Luqman told his son not to turn his cheek from people in contempt, nor walk through the earth exultantly, for Allah does not love anyone self-deluded and boastful. He told him to be moderate in his pace and to lower his voice, since the most disagreeable of sounds is the braying of donkeys.

references.label: Surah Luqman 31:18-19
references.gist: Luqman closes his advice by warning against arrogance in bearing and voice, and commending a moderate walk and a lowered voice.

name: Talut and Jalut (Saul and Goliath)
summary: The Israelites asked their prophet to appoint them a king, and Talut was chosen despite objections about his lineage and wealth; his small band, tested at a river, faced Jalut's larger army and defeated it, with Jalut killed by a young man.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:246-251
references.gist: The Israelites ask for a king, Talut is chosen and confirmed by a sign, his soldiers are tested at a river, and the faithful remnant defeats Jalut's army.

tale.intro: Neither the prophet nor most of those involved are named by the Quran in this passage itself, though the young man who kills Jalut is identified elsewhere in the Quran as Dawud, whose own tale is told separately on this site.

chapters.heading: The Israelites Ask for a King
chapters.narrative: After the time of Moses, the chiefs of the Children of Israel said to a prophet of theirs, 'Send to us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah.' He asked whether they might hold back from fighting if it were prescribed for them; they answered, 'Why should we not fight in the cause of Allah when we have been driven from our homes and our children?' Yet when fighting was prescribed, they turned away, except for a few - and Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:246
references.gist: The Israelites ask their prophet for a king so they can fight in Allah's cause, but most turn away once fighting is actually prescribed.

chapters.heading: Talut is Chosen Despite Objections
chapters.narrative: Their prophet told them Allah had sent Talut (Saul) to them as king. They objected, 'How can he have kingship over us when we are more worthy of it than he, and he has not been given any measure of wealth?' The prophet answered that Allah had chosen him over them and increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature, and that Allah gives His sovereignty to whom He wills.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:247
references.gist: The people object to Talut's kingship over his lack of wealth and lineage; the prophet answers that Allah chose him and gave him knowledge and stature.

chapters.heading: The Sign of the Ark's Return
chapters.narrative: Their prophet told them a sign of Talut's kingship would be that the chest (the Ark) would come to them, carried by the angels, containing assurance from their Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron had left behind - a sign for them if they were believers.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:248
references.gist: The confirming sign of Talut's kingship is the return of the Ark, carried by angels, containing a remnant of what the families of Moses and Aaron had left.

chapters.heading: The Test at the River
chapters.narrative: When Talut set out with his soldiers, he told them Allah would test them with a river: whoever drank from it would not be of him, and whoever did not taste it would be of him, except for one who took a sip in the hollow of his hand. Most of them drank from it, except for a few.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:249
references.gist: Talut tests his soldiers at a river; nearly all drink freely and are excluded, except a small number who abstain or take only a sip.

chapters.heading: The Small Group Facing Jalut
chapters.narrative: When the small remaining group went forth to face Jalut (Goliath) and his soldiers, they prayed, 'Our Lord, pour upon us patience, plant firmly our feet, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.'

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:250
references.gist: The small band that remains faithful goes to face Jalut's larger army, asking Allah for patience, firmness, and victory.

chapters.heading: Jalut's Defeat
chapters.narrative: By Allah's permission, they defeated Jalut's army, and Dawud killed Jalut; Allah gave Dawud kingship and prophethood and taught him what He willed. The young man who struck down Jalut here is Dawud, whose fuller story - as a prophet in his own right - is told separately on this site.

references.label: Surah Al-Baqarah 2:251
references.gist: The small army defeats Jalut's forces by Allah's permission, and Dawud kills Jalut, after which Allah grants him kingship and prophethood.

name: The People of the Garden (Ashab al-Jannah)
summary: The owners of a fruitful garden secretly conspired to harvest it early at dawn so no poor person could share in it, but woke to find it destroyed, and were left in remorse - except the most moderate among them, who had urged them to glorify Allah.

references.label: Surah Al-Qalam 68:17-33
references.gist: Garden owners plot to harvest their garden in secret to exclude the poor, wake to find it destroyed overnight, and are left in mutual blame and regret.

tale.intro: The Quran presents this as a parable of a test, comparable to a real trial the garden's owners faced.

chapters.heading: A Test Like the Owners of the Garden
chapters.narrative: Allah says He tried the people of Makkah as He tried the companions of a garden, who swore they would harvest its fruit in the early morning, without qualifying their oath with 'if Allah wills.' So an affliction from their Lord came upon the garden while they slept, and it became as though it had been completely reaped.

references.label: Surah Al-Qalam 68:17-20
references.gist: The garden's owners swear to harvest it at dawn without exception, and an affliction destroys the garden overnight while they sleep.

chapters.heading: Setting Out to Exclude the Poor
chapters.narrative: In the morning they called to one another, 'Go early to your crop if you mean to harvest it,' and they set out lowering their voices, saying, 'No poor person will enter it upon you today.' They went out early, determined and confident in their own ability.

references.label: Surah Al-Qalam 68:21-25
references.gist: The owners deliberately set out early and quietly, intending to keep the poor from sharing in the harvest.

chapters.heading: Waking to Ruin
chapters.narrative: When they saw the garden, they said, 'We are lost - rather, we have been deprived [of it entirely].'

references.label: Surah Al-Qalam 68:26-27
references.gist: The owners arrive to find the garden destroyed and realize they have lost everything.

chapters.heading: The Best Among Them
chapters.narrative: The most moderate among them said, 'Did I not tell you to glorify Allah?' They replied, 'Exalted is our Lord - indeed, we were wrongdoers.' They then turned to blaming one another.

references.label: Surah Al-Qalam 68:28-30
references.gist: The most moderate of the group reminds them he had urged them to glorify Allah, and they admit their wrongdoing before turning on each other in blame.

chapters.heading: Regret and Hope
chapters.narrative: They said, 'Woe to us - we were indeed transgressors. Perhaps our Lord will give us something better than this in exchange; indeed we are turning to our Lord in hope.' Allah says such is the punishment of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.

references.label: Surah Al-Qalam 68:31-33
references.gist: The owners admit their transgression and express hope that Allah will give them better in exchange, while Allah notes this worldly punishment is lesser than what awaits in the Hereafter.

name: Qarun (Korah)
summary: A man from the people of Moses given immense wealth, who grew arrogant and credited his riches to his own knowledge, rejected the advice to also seek the Hereafter and do good, and was ultimately swallowed by the earth along with his home.

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:76-82
references.gist: Qarun's immense wealth leads him to arrogance and a claim that his fortune came from his own knowledge; he rejects the advice given to him and is swallowed by the earth.

chapters.heading: Immense Wealth, Immense Arrogance
chapters.narrative: Qarun was from the people of Moses, but he oppressed them. Allah had given him treasures whose keys alone would burden a band of strong men to carry. His own people told him, 'Do not exult - Allah does not like the exultant.'

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:76
references.gist: Qarun, from the people of Moses, is given extraordinary wealth and warned by his people not to exult in it, since Allah does not love the exultant.

chapters.heading: The Advice He Rejected
chapters.narrative: He was told to seek, through what Allah had given him, the home of the Hereafter, without forgetting his own share of this world; to do good as Allah had done good to him; and not to seek corruption in the land, for Allah does not love corrupters. Qarun answered, 'I was only given this because of knowledge I have.' The Quran notes he did not consider that Allah had destroyed generations before him who were greater than him in power and in wealth, though the guilty are not questioned about their sins in that way.

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:77-78
references.gist: Qarun is advised to balance seeking the Hereafter with his worldly share and to do good and avoid corruption; he instead credits his wealth entirely to his own knowledge.

chapters.heading: Envy and Insight
chapters.narrative: When Qarun went out before his people in his finery, those who desired the life of this world said, 'If only we had what Qarun has been given - he is truly a man of great fortune.' But those who had been given knowledge said, 'Woe to you - the reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteousness, and none are granted it except the patient.'

references.label: Surah Al-Qasas 28:79-80
